## Chapter 07: Collections Framework

> **Reading Time:** ~55 minutes | **Page Equivalent:** ~22 pages  
> **Prerequisites:** Chapters 01–06  
> **Interview Weight:** ★★★★★

---

## Section 1: Beginner Explanation

### What Is the Java Collections Framework?

The Collections Framework (JCF) is a unified architecture for representing and manipulating groups of objects. Introduced in Java 1.2, it provides interfaces, implementations, and algorithms for data structures.

```
                    Java Collections Framework
                    ══════════════════════════

                         Iterable<T>
                             │
                         Collection<E>
                        ╱    │    ╲
                       ╱     │     ╲
                  List<E>  Set<E>  Queue<E>
                    │        │        │
              ┌─────┼─────┐  │   ┌────┼────┐
              │     │     │  │   │    │    │
          ArrayList Linked  │  │ Priority Array
                  List    │  │ Queue  Deque
                          │  │
                    HashSet  │
                    Linked   │
                    HashSet  │
                    TreeSet  │
                             │
                         Map<K,V>  (NOT a Collection!)
                             │
                    ┌────────┼────────┐
                    │        │        │
                HashMap  LinkedHash  TreeMap
                         Map
```

### Core Interfaces at a Glance

| Interface | Ordered? | Duplicate? | Null? | Access |
|-----------|----------|------------|-------|--------|
| `List` | Yes (index) | Yes | Yes | Random access |
| `Set` | No* | No | 1 null (HashSet) | Contains check |
| `Queue` | Yes (FIFO) | Yes | Varies | Head/tail |
| `Deque` | Yes (both ends) | Yes | Varies | Both ends |
| `Map` | No* | Keys: No | 1 null key (HashMap) | Key lookup |

*LinkedHashSet/LinkedHashMap maintain insertion order. TreeSet/TreeMap maintain sorted order.

### Choosing the Right Collection

```
Need key-value pairs?
  YES → Map
    Need sorted keys? → TreeMap
    Need insertion order? → LinkedHashMap
    Default → HashMap
  NO ↓

Need unique elements?
  YES → Set
    Need sorted? → TreeSet
    Need insertion order? → LinkedHashSet
    Default → HashSet
  NO ↓

Need FIFO processing?
  YES → Queue / ArrayDeque
  NO ↓

Need indexed access?
  YES → List
    Frequent insert/delete in middle? → LinkedList
    Everything else → ArrayList
```

## Section 2: Internal Working

### Collection Interface Hierarchy (Methods)

```java
// Iterable — can be traversed
interface Iterable<T> {
    Iterator<T> iterator();
    void forEach(Consumer<? super T> action);     // Java 8+
    Spliterator<T> spliterator();                    // Java 8+
}

// Collection — group of objects
interface Collection<E> extends Iterable<E> {
    int size();
    boolean isEmpty();
    boolean add(E e);
    boolean remove(Object o);
    boolean contains(Object o);
    Iterator<E> iterator();
    Object[] toArray();
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c);
    boolean removeAll(Collection<?> c);
    boolean retainAll(Collection<?> c);
    void clear();
    // Java 8+ bulk operations:
    default boolean removeIf(Predicate<? super E> filter);
    default Stream<E> stream();
    default Stream<E> parallelStream();
}

// List — indexed collection
interface List<E> extends Collection<E> {
    E get(int index);
    E set(int index, E element);
    void add(int index, E element);
    E remove(int index);
    int indexOf(Object o);
    int lastIndexOf(Object o);
    List<E> subList(int from, int to);
    // Java 8+: sort, replaceAll, spliterator overrides
}

// Set — no duplicates
interface Set<E> extends Collection<E> {
    // Same methods as Collection — semantics differ (no duplicates)
}

// Map — key-value pairs (NOT a Collection)
interface Map<K, V> {
    int size();
    boolean isEmpty();
    boolean containsKey(Object key);
    boolean containsValue(Object value);
    V get(Object key);
    V put(K key, V value);
    V remove(Object key);
    void putAll(Map<? extends K, ? extends V> m);
    void clear();
    Set<K> keySet();
    Collection<V> values();
    Set<Map.Entry<K,V>> entrySet();
    // Java 8+: getOrDefault, putIfAbsent, compute, merge, forEach
}
```

### Iterator and Fail-Fast Behavior

```java
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("A", "B", "C"));
Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();

while (it.hasNext()) {
    String item = it.next();
    if (item.equals("B")) {
        it.remove();        // OK — uses iterator's remove()
        // list.remove(item);  // WRONG — ConcurrentModificationException!
    }
}
```

**Fail-fast mechanism:**
```
ArrayList maintains:
  modCount = 0  (incremented on every structural modification)

Iterator stores:
  expectedModCount = 0  (snapshot at creation time)

On each next()/remove():
  if (modCount != expectedModCount) → ConcurrentModificationException
```

**Important:** Fail-fast is best-effort, not a concurrency guarantee. Only detects modification during iteration, not across threads.

### Comparable vs Comparator

```java
// Comparable: natural ordering (class implements it)
public class User implements Comparable<User> {
    private String name;
    public int compareTo(User other) {
        return this.name.compareTo(other.name);
    }
}
TreeSet<User> users = new TreeSet<>();  // uses compareTo()

// Comparator: external/custom ordering
Comparator<User> byAge = Comparator.comparingInt(User::getAge);
TreeSet<User> users = new TreeSet<>(byAge);

// Java 8+ Comparator utilities:
Comparator<User> chained = Comparator
    .comparing(User::getLastName)
    .thenComparing(User::getFirstName)
    .thenComparingInt(User::getAge)
    .reversed();
```

### Collections Utility Class

```java
// Unmodifiable views (any modification throws UnsupportedOperationException)
List<String> immutable = Collections.unmodifiableList(mutableList);

// Synchronized wrappers (every method synchronized — prefer Concurrent collections)
List<String> sync = Collections.synchronizedList(list);

// Singleton and empty
List<String> empty = Collections.emptyList();
Set<String> singleton = Collections.singleton("only");

// Sorting and searching (List must be sorted for binarySearch)
Collections.sort(list);
Collections.binarySearch(list, key);

// Java 9+ factory methods (truly immutable)
List<String> fixed = List.of("A", "B", "C");     // no null, no modification
Map<String, Integer> map = Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2);
Set<String> set = Set.of("X", "Y", "Z");
```

---

## Section 3: Under the Hood

### Java 9+ Immutable Collections

```java
List<String> list = List.of("A", "B", "C");

// Internal structure (not ArrayList!):
// - Fixed-size array stored directly
// - No modCount, no capacity field, no growth logic
// - add/remove → UnsupportedOperationException
// - null elements → NullPointerException at creation
// - Memory: ~40 bytes vs ArrayList's ~80+ bytes for 3 elements
```

### Stream Pipeline Integration

```java
// Collections are stream sources
List<Integer> result = list.stream()
    .filter(n -> n > 0)
    .map(n -> n * 2)
    .sorted()
    .distinct()
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// Collectors for grouping
Map<String, List<Order>> byStatus = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::getStatus));

// Partitioning
Map<Boolean, List<Order>> partitioned = orders.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.getAmount() > 1000));
```

### Spliterator (Java 8+)

```
Spliterator = Splitting Iterator (for parallel streams)

Characteristics flags:
  ORDERED      — elements have defined encounter order
  DISTINCT     — no duplicates
  SORTED       — elements sorted
  SIZED        — knows exact element count
  NONNULL      — no null elements
  IMMUTABLE    — cannot be modified
  CONCURRENT   — can be modified concurrently
  SUBSIZED     — split parts are SIZED too

ArrayList Spliterator: ORDERED | SIZED | SUBSIZED
HashMap Spliterator:   DISTINCT | CONCURRENT (weakly)
```

### Time Complexity Summary

| Operation | ArrayList | LinkedList | HashSet | TreeSet | HashMap | TreeMap |
|-----------|-----------|------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|
| add | O(1)* | O(1) | O(1) | O(log n) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| remove | O(n) | O(1)** | O(1) | O(log n) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| get/contains | O(1) | O(n) | O(1) | O(log n) | O(1) | O(log n) |
| iterate | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |

*Amortized O(1) for ArrayList add (occasional resize).  
**O(1) only if you have the Node reference; O(n) to find it.

## Section 4: Production Use Cases

### Use Case 1: Choosing Collections in REST API Layer

```java
// Response DTOs: use List for ordered results
public class SearchResponse {
    private List<UserDto> results;     // ordered by relevance
    private int totalCount;
}

// Lookup tables: use Map
private final Map<String, Currency> currencyCache = new HashMap<>();

// Deduplication: use Set
Set<String> uniqueEmails = new HashSet<>(emailList);

// Sorted leaderboard: use TreeMap
TreeMap<Integer, String> leaderboard = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
```

### Use Case 2: Immutable Collections for Thread Safety

```java
// Defensive copy on construction (immutable DTO)
public class ConfigSnapshot {
    private final List<String> allowedRegions;
    
    public ConfigSnapshot(List<String> regions) {
        this.allowedRegions = List.copyOf(regions);  // Java 10+ immutable copy
    }
    
    public List<String> getAllowedRegions() {
        return allowedRegions;  // safe — cannot be modified
    }
}
```

### Use Case 3: Bulk Operations for Data Processing

```java
// Remove all expired orders in one pass
orders.removeIf(order -> order.getExpiryDate().isBefore(LocalDate.now()));

// Compute map in-place
productCounts.computeIfAbsent(productId, k -> new AtomicInteger(0)).incrementAndGet();

// Merge for aggregation
Map<String, BigDecimal> totals = transactions.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.toMap(
        Transaction::getCategory,
        Transaction::getAmount,
        BigDecimal::add  // merge function for duplicate keys
    ));
```

### Use Case 4: EnumSet and EnumMap for Enums

```java
// When keys are enum values — always use EnumSet/EnumMap
// Internally: bit vector (EnumSet) or array (EnumMap) — faster than HashSet/HashMap

EnumSet<DayOfWeek> weekends = EnumSet.of(DayOfWeek.SATURDAY, DayOfWeek.SUNDAY);
EnumMap<Status, String> statusLabels = new EnumMap<>(Status.class);
// O(1) operations, zero hashing overhead, memory efficient
```

## Section 5: Performance Considerations

### ArrayList vs LinkedList in Practice

```
Benchmark: 1 million operations on 100K element collection

                    ArrayList    LinkedList
Add at end          5ms          8ms
Add at beginning    2000ms       5ms
Get by index        2ms          500,000ms
Contains/search     200ms        500,000ms
Iterate             10ms         15ms
Memory per element  4 bytes      24 bytes (node overhead)

Verdict: ArrayList wins 95% of use cases.
LinkedList only when: frequent insert/delete at BOTH ends with iterator (Deque).
```

### Initial Capacity Sizing

```java
// BAD: default capacity 10, grows by 1.5x each resize
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) orders.add(new Order());  // ~17 resize/copy operations

// GOOD: pre-size to expected count
List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(100_000);  // zero resizes

// HashMap: default 16 buckets, load factor 0.75
// Resize at 12 elements → 32 → 64 → ...
Map<String, User> users = new HashMap<>(expectedSize * 4 / 3 + 1);  // avoid resize
```

### Boxing Cost in Collections

```java
// 1 million Integer objects = ~24 MB (16 header + 4 value + 4 padding)
List<Integer> boxed = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) boxed.add(i);

// Primitive: 4 MB
int[] primitive = new int[1_000_000];

// Libraries: Eclipse Collections, FastUtil, HPPC
IntArrayList primitive = new IntArrayList();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) primitive.add(i);
```

## Section 6: Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1: Using LinkedList as Default List

```java
List<String> list = new LinkedList<>();  // Almost never correct
// Use ArrayList unless you specifically need Deque operations
```

### Mistake 2: Modifying Collection During Enhanced For-Loop

```java
for (String item : list) {
    if (item.equals("remove-me"))
        list.remove(item);  // ConcurrentModificationException!
}
// Fix: iterator.remove() or removeIf()
list.removeIf(item -> item.equals("remove-me"));
```

### Mistake 3: Using Raw Types

```java
Map cache = new HashMap();  // Raw type — no type safety
cache.put("key", 42);
String val = (String) cache.get("key");  // ClassCastException!
```

### Mistake 4: HashMap get() Without null Check

```java
// get() returns null for missing key AND for null values!
String value = map.get("key");
if (value.equals("expected")) { }  // NPE if key missing!

// Safe alternatives:
if ("expected".equals(map.get("key"))) { }  // null-safe
String value = map.getOrDefault("key", "default");
boolean exists = map.containsKey("key");
```

### Mistake 5: Not Overriding equals/hashCode for Set/Map Keys

```java
class User { String name; }  // No equals/hashCode!

Set<User> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new User("Alice"));
set.add(new User("Alice"));  // DUPLICATE! Different hash codes
set.size();  // 2 — not 1!
```

## Section 8: Tricky Follow-Up Questions

### FQ1: "What is the load factor in HashMap? What happens when it's exceeded?"

Load factor (default 0.75) = threshold for resize. When `size > capacity × loadFactor`, HashMap doubles bucket array and rehashes all entries. Trade-off: higher load factor = less memory but more collisions; lower = more memory but fewer collisions.

### FQ2: "Can you add null to a TreeMap?"

No. `TreeMap.put(null, value)` throws `NullPointerException` because null cannot be compared (no natural ordering for null). `HashMap` allows one null key.

### FQ3: "What is the difference between Collections.synchronizedList() and CopyOnWriteArrayList?"

`synchronizedList`: every operation synchronized — thread-safe but contended. `CopyOnWriteArrayList`: copies entire array on write — great for read-heavy, rare-write scenarios (listener lists). Writes are O(n) due to copying.

### FQ4: "How does HashSet store elements if it doesn't have add(E) with uniqueness logic?"

HashSet is a wrapper around HashMap — elements stored as keys with a dummy `PRESENT` object as value. Uniqueness enforced by HashMap's key uniqueness.

### FQ5: "What is weakly consistent iteration?"

Used by ConcurrentHashMap's iterators. Never throws ConcurrentModificationException. May or may not reflect modifications during iteration. Guaranteed to traverse elements as they existed at iterator creation, plus some subsequent modifications.

## Section 9: Senior Engineer Answers

### A1: Collection Selection

> "My default choices: ArrayList for lists — cache-friendly contiguous memory, O(1) random access, and modern CPUs prefetch array elements efficiently. HashMap for key-value — O(1) operations with good hash function. HashSet for uniqueness — backed by HashMap. I only deviate when requirements demand it: TreeMap when I need sorted keys or range queries (`subMap`, `headMap`). LinkedHashMap when I need LRU cache behavior with `removeEldestEntry()`. ConcurrentHashMap for shared mutable state across threads. I never use LinkedList as a general-purpose List — ArrayList outperforms it in almost every scenario including insert-at-front for small lists, because CPU cache locality dominates algorithmic complexity."

### A2: equals/hashCode Contract

> "The contract is: if two objects are equal per `equals()`, they MUST have the same `hashCode()`. The converse is not required — hash collisions are allowed. Violating this breaks HashMap and HashSet — equal objects placed in different buckets, making lookups fail. I always use IDE generation or Lombok `@EqualsAndHashCode` for DTOs used as map keys or set elements. For JPA entities, I use only the primary key in equals/hashCode — never fields that can change, because modifying a hashCode after insertion into a HashMap makes the object unfindable."

---

## Section 10: Technical Lead Answers

### A1: Collection Standards for Codebase

> "I established collection usage standards for our 80-service codebase after finding inconsistent patterns causing performance issues and bugs. Rules: 1) ArrayList as default List — ArchUnit test fails on `new LinkedList<>()`. 2) All DTOs used as HashMap keys must have `@EqualsAndHashCode`. 3) No raw types — enforced by Checkstyle. 4) Defensive copies: all public API methods returning collections use `List.copyOf()` or `Collections.unmodifiableList()`. 5) Initial capacity: any collection expected to hold >100 elements must specify initial capacity. 6) Concurrent collections mandatory for shared state — no `Collections.synchronized*` in service layer. These standards eliminated three categories of bugs: ClassCastException from raw types, duplicate entries in HashSet from missing equals/hashCode, and ConcurrentModificationException from unsafe iteration."

---

## Section 11: Real Production Incident Examples

### Incident 1: LinkedList Causing 10x Latency

**Company:** Logistics platform (Uber-scale)  
**Symptom:** Route calculation API P99 = 3 seconds (expected 300ms)  
**Root Cause:** Developer used `LinkedList<Waypoint>` for 50K waypoints. `get(i)` in Dijkstra's algorithm = O(n) per access = O(n²) total.

**Fix:** Changed to `ArrayList<Waypoint>`. P99 dropped to 280ms.

### Incident 2: HashMap Memory Leak via Key Mutation

**Company:** E-commerce (Walmart-scale)  
**Symptom:** Cache hit rate dropped from 95% to 40% after a deployment

**Root Cause:**
```java
class CacheKey {
    String category;
    // equals/hashCode based on category
}
CacheKey key = new CacheKey("electronics");
cache.put(key, data);
key.setCategory("books");  // MUTATED after insertion!
cache.get(key);  // MISS — hash bucket changed
```

**Fix:** Made cache keys immutable. Added `@Immutable` ArchUnit rule.

## Section 12: Revision Notes

### Must-Know Facts

```
HIERARCHY: Iterable → Collection → List/Set/Queue; Map (separate)
DEFAULT CHOICES: ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet

FAIL-FAST: modCount check → ConcurrentModificationException
  Fix: iterator.remove() or removeIf() or ConcurrentHashMap

equals/hashCode: equal objects → same hashCode (required for HashMap/HashSet)
JPA entities: equals/hashCode on ID only

COMPLEXITIES:
  ArrayList: get O(1), add-end O(1)*, add-middle O(n)
  LinkedList: get O(n), add-both-ends O(1)
  HashMap/HashSet: O(1) average, O(n) worst (collisions)
  TreeMap/TreeSet: O(log n) all operations

Java 9+: List.of(), Map.of(), Set.copyOf() — truly immutable
EnumSet/EnumMap: always prefer for enum keys/values
```

## Chapter 08: ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap, ConcurrentHashMap — Source-Level Deep Dive

> **Reading Time:** ~65 minutes | **Page Equivalent:** ~25 pages  
> **Prerequisites:** Chapter 07 (Collections Framework)  
> **Interview Weight:** ★★★★★ (Most frequently asked Java interview topic)

## Section 1: Beginner Explanation

### Why This Chapter Exists

Interviewers at Amazon, Google, Goldman Sachs, and Uber routinely ask: *"Explain the internal working of HashMap"* and *"ArrayList vs LinkedList."* This chapter goes to the **source code level** — the actual fields, algorithms, and resize mechanisms inside OpenJDK implementations.

### ArrayList — Resizable Array

Think of ArrayList as a Java wrapper around a dynamic array:

```java
ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("A");  // [A]
list.add("B");  // [A, B]
list.add("C");  // [A, B, C]
list.get(1);    // "B" — direct array index access
```

### LinkedList — Doubly Linked Nodes

```java
LinkedList<String> list = new LinkedList<>();
// Internally: Node { prev, item, next } chain
list.add("A");     // A <-> null
list.add("B");     // A <-> B <-> null
list.addFirst("Z"); // Z <-> A <-> B
```

### HashMap — Hash Table with Buckets

```java
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("Alice", 30);   // hash("Alice") → bucket index → store entry
map.get("Alice");       // hash("Alice") → same bucket → return 30
```

### ConcurrentHashMap — Thread-Safe HashMap

```java
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
map.put("Alice", 30);           // Thread-safe without full synchronization
map.compute("Bob", (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);  // Atomic update
```

---

## Section 2: Internal Working

### ArrayList Internal Structure

```java
// OpenJDK ArrayList source (simplified)
public class ArrayList<E> {
    private static final int DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 10;
    
    transient Object[] elementData;  // The actual backing array
    private int size;                // Number of elements (NOT capacity)
    
    // add(E e) — amortized O(1)
    public boolean add(E e) {
        ensureCapacityInternal(size + 1);
        elementData[size++] = e;
        return true;
    }
    
    // ensureCapacity — grow when needed
    private void grow(int minCapacity) {
        int oldCapacity = elementData.length;
        int newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1);  // 1.5x growth
        if (newCapacity < minCapacity) newCapacity = minCapacity;
        elementData = Arrays.copyOf(elementData, newCapacity);
    }
    
    // get(int index) — O(1)
    public E get(int index) {
        rangeCheck(index);
        return (E) elementData[index];
    }
    
    // add(int index, E element) — O(n)
    public void add(int index, E element) {
        rangeCheckForAdd(index);
        ensureCapacityInternal(size + 1);
        System.arraycopy(elementData, index, elementData, index + 1, size - index);
        elementData[index] = element;
        size++;
    }
    
    // remove(int index) — O(n)
    public E remove(int index) {
        rangeCheck(index);
        E oldValue = (E) elementData[index];
        int numMoved = size - index - 1;
        if (numMoved > 0)
            System.arraycopy(elementData, index + 1, elementData, index, numMoved);
        elementData[--size] = null;  // GC help
        return oldValue;
    }
}
```

**ArrayList growth visualization:**
```
Initial: capacity=10, size=0
[A][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ][ ]

After 10 adds: size=10, capacity=10 (full)
[A][B][C][D][E][F][G][H][I][J]

Add K: grow! new capacity = 10 + 10/2 = 15
[A][B][C][D][E][F][G][H][I][J][K][ ][ ][ ][ ]
                              size=11, capacity=15

After 5 more adds: size=15, capacity=15 (full)
Grow: 15 + 7 = 22
```

### LinkedList Internal Structure

```java
// OpenJDK LinkedList source (simplified)
public class LinkedList<E> {
    
    transient int size = 0;
    transient Node<E> first;  // head
    transient Node<E> last;   // tail
    
    private static class Node<E> {
        E item;
        Node<E> next;
        Node<E> prev;
        
        Node(Node<E> prev, E element, Node<E> next) {
            this.item = element;
            this.next = next;
            this.prev = prev;
        }
    }
    
    // add(E e) — O(1) — append to tail
    public boolean add(E e) {
        linkLast(e);
        return true;
    }
    
    void linkLast(E e) {
        Node<E> l = last;
        Node<E> newNode = new Node<>(l, e, null);
        last = newNode;
        if (l == null) first = newNode;
        else l.next = newNode;
        size++;
    }
    
    // get(int index) — O(n) — traverse from closer end
    public E get(int index) {
        if (index < (size >> 1))
            return node(index).item;          // forward from head
        else
            return node(size - 1 - index).item; // backward from tail (still O(n))
    }
    
    // add(int index, E element) — O(n) to find position + O(1) to link
    public void add(int index, E element) {
        Node<E> succ = node(index);  // O(n) traversal
        linkBefore(element, succ);   // O(1) pointer manipulation
    }
}
```

**LinkedList memory per element:**
```
ArrayList:  4 bytes (reference in Object[])
LinkedList: 24 bytes (Node object)
  - Object header: 12 bytes
  - item reference: 4 bytes
  - next reference: 4 bytes
  - prev reference: 4 bytes
  = 3x memory overhead per element
```

### HashMap Internal Structure

```java
// OpenJDK HashMap source (Java 8+, simplified)
public class HashMap<K, V> {
    
    static final int DEFAULT_INITIAL_CAPACITY = 16;
    static final float DEFAULT_LOAD_FACTOR = 0.75f;
    static final int TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8;
    static final int UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6;
    
    transient Node<K,V>[] table;  // Bucket array
    transient int size;
    int threshold;                 // capacity * loadFactor
    final float loadFactor;
    
    // Node (singly linked list in each bucket)
    static class Node<K,V> {
        final int hash;
        final K key;
        V value;
        Node<K,V> next;
    }
    
    // TreeNode (red-black tree for collision-heavy buckets)
    static final class TreeNode<K,V> extends LinkedHashMap.Entry<K,V> {
        TreeNode<K,V> parent, left, right, prev;
        boolean red;
    }
}
```

**HashMap put operation flow:**
```
put("Alice", 30)
     │
     ▼
1. hash("Alice") = hashCode() ^ (hashCode() >>> 16)
     │  Spreads high bits into low bits (reduces collisions when
     │  table size is power of 2 — only low bits used for index)
     ▼
2. index = hash & (table.length - 1)   // equivalent to hash % length
     │  table.length=16: index = hash & 15 (last 4 bits)
     ▼
3. Check table[index]:
     ├── null → create new Node, done
     ├── same hash + equals(key) → update value, done
     └── collision → traverse linked list
           ├── found match → update value
           └── end of list → append new Node
                 └── if chain length ≥ 8 → TREEIFY to Red-Black Tree
     ▼
4. size++. If size > threshold → RESIZE (double table, rehash all)
```

**HashMap bucket visualization:**
```
table (capacity = 8):
┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
│ 0 │ 1 │ 2 │ 3 │ 4 │ 5 │ 6 │ 7 │
└─┬─┘ └─┬─┘ └───┘ └─┬─┘ └───┘ └─┬─┘ └───┘
  │     │           │           │
 null  Node       null        TreeNode
       ↓                       ↙   ↘
      Node(K2)              Node   Node
       ↓
      null
       
Bucket 1: linked list (few collisions)
Bucket 6: red-black tree (≥8 collisions → treeified)
```

**Resize (rehash) operation:**
```
Before resize: capacity=16, threshold=12, size=13
  → Double capacity to 32
  → Recompute index for EVERY entry (hash & 31 instead of hash & 15)
  → Entries may move to different buckets
  → O(n) operation — expensive!

After resize: capacity=32, threshold=24
```

### ConcurrentHashMap Internal Structure (Java 8+)

```java
// OpenJDK ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+, simplified)
public class ConcurrentHashMap<K,V> {
    
    transient volatile Node<K,V>[] table;
    private transient volatile int sizeCtl;  // control state
    
    // Node with volatile value (visibility across threads)
    static class Node<K,V> {
        final int hash;
        final K key;
        volatile V val;       // volatile!
        volatile Node<K,V> next;
    }
    
    // put(K key, V value) — thread-safe without full map lock
    public V put(K key, V value) { ... }
    
    // Uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for lock-free bucket initialization
    // Uses synchronized block on FIRST NODE of bucket for updates
    // NOT lock-striping like Java 7 (16 Segment locks)
}
```

**Java 7 vs Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap:**
```
Java 7: Segment[] array (16 segments default)
  ┌─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐
  │Segment 0│Segment 1│Segment 2│  Each segment = mini HashMap with ReentrantLock
  │ HashMap │ HashMap │ HashMap │  Lock granularity: 1/16 of map
  └─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘

Java 8: Node[] array (like HashMap) with per-bucket locking
  ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
  │ 0 │ 1 │ 2 │ 3 │ 4 │ 5 │ 6 │ 7 │
  └───┘ └─┬─┘ └───┘ └───┘ └─┬─┘ └───┘
         LOCK           LOCK
  Lock granularity: single bucket (finer than Java 7)
  + CAS for read/insert into empty buckets (lock-free)
  + synchronized on first node for updates in populated buckets
  + TreeNode (red-black) for collision-heavy buckets
```

---

## Section 3: Under the Hood

### HashMap hash() Function — Why XOR with Shifted Bits

```java
static final int hash(Object key) {
    int h;
    return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}

// Example: String "Alice" hashCode = 924584536 = 0x371F4F78
//   h         = 0011 0111 0001 1111 0100 1111 0111 1000
//   h >>> 16  = 0000 0000 0000 0000 0011 0111 0001 1111
//   h ^ h>>>16 = 0011 0111 0001 1111 0111 1010 1000 0111
//
// Without spread: only low 4 bits used for index (when capacity=16)
//   → only 16 possible indices regardless of hashCode quality
// With spread: high bits influence low bits via XOR
//   → better distribution across buckets
```

### String hashCode() Implementation

```java
// String.java
public int hashCode() {
    int h = hash;  // cached after first computation
    if (h == 0 && value.length > 0) {
        for (int i = 0; i < value.length; i++) {
            h = 31 * h + val[i];  // h = 31^n * char[0] + ... + char[n]
        }
        hash = h;
    }
    return h;
}
// Why 31? Prime number → fewer collisions; 31*i = (i<<5)-i → JVM optimizes to bit shift
```

### Red-Black Tree in HashMap (Java 8+)

When a bucket has ≥8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD), the linked list converts to a red-black tree:

```
Before treeify (bucket with 8+ nodes):
  [hash=100] → [hash=116] → [hash=132] → ... → [hash=228]
  Lookup: O(n) — traverse list comparing hash + equals

After treeify:
       [hash=164]
       /          \
  [hash=132]    [hash=196]
    /    \          \
[100]  [hash=148] [hash=228]
  Lookup: O(log n) — tree traversal
```

**When treeify is NOT done:**
- Table size < 64 → resize instead of treeify (cheaper to double buckets)
- Tree has ≤6 nodes → untreeify back to linked list

### ConcurrentHashMap: put() Step by Step

```
put(key, value):
  1. Compute hash (same as HashMap)
  2. If table is null → initialize via CAS (compare-and-swap, lock-free)
  3. Find bucket index
  4. If bucket is empty → CAS insert new Node (lock-free)
  5. If bucket is being treeified → wait (synchronized on bin)
  6. If first node hash is MOVED (resize in progress) → help resize + retry
  7. Otherwise → synchronized(firstNode) {
       traverse list/tree
       if key found → update value
       else → add new node
       if count ≥ TREEIFY_THRESHOLD → treeify
     }
  8. If size exceeds threshold → transfer (resize) — multiple threads can help
```

### ConcurrentHashMap: size() — Why It's Approximate

```java
// size() returns int — may be approximate during concurrent updates
public int size() {
    // Sums per-node element counts using baseCount + CounterCell[] (striped counting)
    // Not synchronized — trade-off: fast reads, approximate count
}

// For exact count: mappingCount() returns long (Java 8+)
public long mappingCount() { ... }
```

## Section 4: Production Use Cases

### Use Case 1: HashMap as In-Memory Cache with LRU Eviction

```java
// LinkedHashMap with access-order and eldest removal
Map<String, User> cache = new LinkedHashMap<>(1000, 0.75f, true) {
    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, User> eldest) {
        return size() > 10_000;  // evict oldest when > 10K entries
    }
};
// 'true' = access-order (get/put moves entry to tail)
// Eldest = least recently accessed → removed first
```

### Use Case 2: ConcurrentHashMap for Metrics Counters

```java
// Thread-safe request counting per endpoint
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> requestCounts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

public void recordRequest(String endpoint) {
    requestCounts.computeIfAbsent(endpoint, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();
}

// LongAdder > AtomicLong for high-contention counting
// Striped internal cells → less CAS contention than single AtomicLong
```

### Use Case 3: ArrayList Pre-Sizing for Known Data Volume

```java
// Database query returns 50K rows
@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.active = true")
List<User> findActiveUsers();  // Returns 50K

// Service layer: pre-sized list for transformation
List<UserDto> dtos = new ArrayList<>(users.size());  // zero resizes
users.forEach(u -> dtos.add(mapper.toDto(u)));
```

### Use Case 4: ConcurrentHashMap.compute() for Atomic Updates

```java
// Inventory reservation — atomic check-and-update
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> inventory = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

boolean reserved = inventory.compute(productId, (key, stock) -> {
    if (stock == null || stock <= 0) return stock;  // no stock
    return stock - 1;  // decrement atomically
}) != null;
// No synchronized block needed — compute() locks single bucket
```

## Section 5: Performance Considerations

### HashMap Initial Capacity Calculation

```java
// Formula: capacity = expectedSize / loadFactor + 1
// For 1000 entries with load factor 0.75:
int capacity = (int) (1000 / 0.75) + 1;  // = 1334 → rounds to 2048 (next power of 2)
Map<String, User> map = new HashMap<>(1334);  // no resize during 1000 puts

// Guava helper:
Map<String, User> map = Maps.newHashMapWithExpectedSize(1000);
```

### HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap Performance

```
Benchmark: 1M put/get operations, 8 threads

                    HashMap       ConcurrentHashMap
Single thread       50ms          80ms (volatile overhead)
8 threads           UNSAFE        120ms
8 threads (sync)    800ms         N/A

ConcurrentHashMap is ~1.5x slower single-threaded but scales linearly.
NEVER use HashMap + synchronized wrapper — 6x slower than CHM.
```

### ArrayList Random Access Performance

```
CPU cache effect on ArrayList vs LinkedList:

ArrayList (contiguous memory):
  [A][B][C][D][E][F][G][H]  ← CPU loads cache line (64 bytes = ~8 references)
  get(0) through get(7): ONE cache miss

LinkedList (scattered nodes):
  Node→Node→Node→Node  ← each node = separate heap allocation
  get(0) through get(7): EIGHT cache misses (pointer chasing)

Result: ArrayList get() is 100-1000x faster in practice despite same Big-O
```

## Section 6: Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1: Using Object as HashMap Key Without Proper hashCode()

```java
// BAD: default hashCode() returns identity hash (memory address)
class MutableKey {
    String value;
    // No equals/hashCode override
}
// Same logical key, different hash codes → duplicates in map

// GOOD: immutable key with proper equals/hashCode
record CacheKey(String category, String region) {}  // auto equals/hashCode
```

### Mistake 2: ConcurrentModificationException with HashMap

```java
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("A", 1);
map.put("B", 2);

// UNSAFE: modifying during iteration
for (String key : map.keySet()) {
    if (key.equals("A")) map.remove(key);  // CME!
}

// SAFE options:
map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getKey().equals("A"));
// OR
Iterator<Map.Entry<String,Integer>> it = map.entrySet().iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    if (it.next().getKey().equals("A")) it.remove();
}
// OR use ConcurrentHashMap (weakly consistent iterator)
```

### Mistake 3: Null Key/Value Confusion

```java
// HashMap: ONE null key allowed, MULTIPLE null values allowed
HashMap<String, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(null, "value");    // OK
map.put("key", null);      // OK
map.get("nonexistent");    // returns null
map.get("key");            // also returns null — AMBIGUOUS!

// ConcurrentHashMap: NO null keys, NO null values
// NullPointerException on put(null, ...) or put(..., null)
```

### Mistake 4: Sublist Memory Leak

```java
List<Integer> big = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) big.add(i);

List<Integer> sub = big.subList(0, 10);  // sub holds reference to ENTIRE big array!
big.clear();  // sub is now undefined behavior
sub.get(0);   // ConcurrentModificationException or wrong data

// Fix: create independent copy
List<Integer> sub = new ArrayList<>(big.subList(0, 10));
```

### Mistake 5: HashMap in Multi-Threaded Context

```java
// DATA RACE — undefined behavior, infinite loops possible (Java 7), lost updates
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();  // NOT thread-safe!
executor.submit(() -> map.put("count", 1));
executor.submit(() -> map.put("count", 2));
// Result: unpredictable — may be 1, 2, or corrupted entry

// FIX: ConcurrentHashMap
Map<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
```

## Section 8: Tricky Follow-Up Questions

### FQ1: "Two keys have the same hashCode. What happens?"

They land in the same bucket. HashMap uses `equals()` after `hashCode()` to distinguish them. Many keys can share a hashCode (collision) — equals() resolves the correct one. If ALL keys collide (adversarial hashCode), performance degrades to O(n) per operation — mitigated by treeification at 8 nodes.

### FQ2: "What is the worst-case time complexity of HashMap get()?"

O(log n) with treeified buckets (Java 8+). O(n) if all keys hash to same bucket and treeification hasn't occurred (table < 64). Before Java 8: O(n) always for collisions.

### FQ3: "Why is HashMap capacity always a power of 2?"

Index calculation: `hash & (capacity - 1)` is faster than `hash % capacity` (bitwise AND vs division). Power of 2 minus 1 creates a bitmask. Trade-off: power-of-2 sizing increases hash collisions (only low bits matter), mitigated by the hash spread function.

### FQ4: "Does ConcurrentHashMap lock the entire map during put()?"

No (Java 8+). It locks only the first node of the target bucket via `synchronized`. Empty bucket inserts use CAS (lock-free). Reads never lock. Resize allows multiple threads to help transfer buckets.

### FQ5: "What happens if you modify an object used as HashMap key after insertion?"

If the modification changes hashCode(), the key becomes unfindable — it's in the old bucket but lookups go to the new bucket. **Keys must be immutable** or their hashCode must not change. This is a common production bug.

## Section 9: Senior Engineer Answers

### A1: HashMap Internal Working

> "HashMap uses an array of buckets, each bucket being a linked list or red-black tree. When you put a key-value pair, HashMap computes hash = key.hashCode() XOR (hashCode >>> 16) to spread bits, then finds the bucket index via hash & (capacity - 1). If the bucket is empty, a new Node is created. If there's a collision, it traverses the linked list comparing hash and equals(). When a bucket reaches 8 nodes and table size is at least 64, the list treeifies to a red-black tree for O(log n) lookup. When size exceeds capacity × load factor (0.75), the table doubles and all entries are rehashed. I always initialize with expected capacity to avoid resize overhead — for 1000 entries, I use `new HashMap<>(1334)`."

### A2: ConcurrentHashMap vs Synchronized HashMap

> "Never use `Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())` for concurrent access — it locks the entire map on every operation, serializing all threads. ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+) uses per-bucket locking: CAS for empty bucket inserts, synchronized on the first node for updates, and volatile reads for lock-free gets. It also supports atomic compound operations: `compute()`, `merge()`, `computeIfAbsent()` — these lock a single bucket, not the entire map. In our metrics service, we use ConcurrentHashMap with LongAdder values for per-endpoint request counting across 16 threads — zero contention compared to synchronized HashMap which dropped throughput by 80%."

---

## Section 10: Technical Lead Answers

### A1: HashMap Key Design Standards

> "I mandated immutable keys for all HashMap/ConcurrentHashMap usage after a production cache invalidation bug where a developer mutated a key object's field after insertion, making 30% of cache entries unfindable. The ADR established: 1) All cache keys must be Java records or Lombok `@Value` classes (immutable by construction). 2) JPA entities must NEVER be used as HashMap keys — their fields change during persistence lifecycle. 3) ArchUnit test: no HashMap fields typed with mutable key classes. 4) For composite keys, use records: `record CacheKey(String tenant, String entity, Long id) {}`. This eliminated an entire category of subtle, hard-to-debug cache misses that were costing us 200ms per affected request."

## Section 11: Real Production Incident Examples

### Incident 1: HashMap Infinite Loop (Java 7)

**Company:** Ad-tech platform  
**Symptom:** Thread stuck at 100% CPU, no progress  
**Stack:** Java 7, HashMap shared between threads (unsafe)

**Root Cause:** Two threads concurrently put into same HashMap bucket during resize. Java 7's transfer mechanism could create circular linked list in bucket → infinite loop on get().

**Fix:** Upgraded to Java 8 (fixed transfer logic) + replaced all shared HashMaps with ConcurrentHashMap.

---

### Incident 2: ArrayList Resize Storm

**Company:** Data processing pipeline (Netflix-scale)  
**Symptom:** Periodic latency spikes every 30 seconds  
**Root Cause:** `new ArrayList<>()` without capacity for 500K element batch. Every 1.5x growth triggered `Arrays.copyOf` — 19 resize operations copying millions of references.

**Fix:** `new ArrayList<>(500_000)`. Latency spikes eliminated.

## Section 12: Revision Notes

### Must-Know Facts

```
ARRAYLIST:
  Backing: Object[] elementData
  Growth: 1.5x (oldCapacity + oldCapacity>>1)
  Default capacity: 10
  get: O(1), add-end: O(1) amortized, add/remove-middle: O(n)

LINKEDLIST:
  Backing: doubly-linked Node { prev, item, next }
  Memory: 24 bytes/element vs 4 bytes in ArrayList
  get: O(n), add-both-ends: O(1)

HASHMAP:
  Backing: Node[] table (buckets)
  Load factor: 0.75, resize: double capacity, rehash all
  Hash: hashCode() ^ (hashCode() >>> 16)
  Index: hash & (capacity - 1)
  Collision: linked list → treeify at 8 nodes (if table ≥ 64)
  Null: one null key, multiple null values allowed

CONCURRENTHASHMAP (Java 8+):
  Per-bucket locking (NOT segment locking like Java 7)
  CAS for empty bucket insert, synchronized(firstNode) for update
  No null keys/values
  compute/merge/computeIfAbsent = atomic per-bucket ops
  Weakly consistent iterators (no CME)

KEY RULE: equal objects → same hashCode; keys must be immutable
```

## Chapter 09: HashSet, TreeMap, PriorityQueue — Advanced Collections Deep Dive

> **Reading Time:** ~50 minutes | **Page Equivalent:** ~20 pages

## Section 1: Beginner Explanation

### HashSet — Unique Elements, Fast Lookup

A `HashSet` stores unique elements with no guaranteed order. It is backed by a `HashMap` where elements are keys and a dummy `PRESENT` object is the value.

```java
Set<String> uniqueUsers = new HashSet<>();
uniqueUsers.add("Alice");   // true (added)
uniqueUsers.add("Bob");     // true (added)
uniqueUsers.add("Alice");   // false (duplicate — not added)
uniqueUsers.contains("Bob"); // true — O(1) average
uniqueUsers.size();          // 2
```

### TreeMap / TreeSet — Sorted Order

`TreeMap` and `TreeSet` maintain elements in **sorted order** using a red-black tree. Every operation is O(log n).

```java
TreeMap<Integer, String> leaderboard = new TreeMap<>();
leaderboard.put(100, "Alice");
leaderboard.put(50, "Bob");
leaderboard.put(200, "Charlie");
// Iteration order: 50→Bob, 100→Alice, 200→Charlie (sorted by key)

TreeMap<Integer, String> topScores = new TreeMap<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
// Iteration: 200→Charlie, 100→Alice, 50→Bob
```

### PriorityQueue — Heap-Based Priority Ordering

A `PriorityQueue` always returns the **highest-priority** element (smallest by default, or custom `Comparator`).

```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();
minHeap.offer(30);
minHeap.offer(10);
minHeap.offer(20);
minHeap.poll();  // 10 (smallest first)

PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
maxHeap.offer(30);
maxHeap.poll();  // 30 (largest first)
```

```
Collection Selection Quick Reference
──────────────────────────────────
Need uniqueness + fast lookup?     → HashSet
Need uniqueness + sorted order?    → TreeSet
Need uniqueness + insertion order? → LinkedHashSet
Need sorted key-value pairs?       → TreeMap
Need key-value + insertion order?  → LinkedHashMap
Need always-min/max element?       → PriorityQueue
Need FIFO?                         → ArrayDeque
```

---

## Section 2: Internal Working

### HashSet — HashMap Wrapper

```java
// OpenJDK HashSet source (simplified)
public class HashSet<E> {
    private transient HashMap<E, Object> map;
    private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();

    public HashSet() {
        map = new HashMap<>();
    }

    public boolean add(E e) {
        return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null;  // null = newly added
    }

    public boolean remove(Object o) {
        return map.remove(o) == PRESENT;
    }

    public boolean contains(Object o) {
        return map.containsKey(o);
    }

    public int size() {
        return map.size();
    }
}
```

**Implication:** Everything about HashMap applies to HashSet — hash function, load factor, resize, treeification, null handling (one null element allowed).

### LinkedHashSet — HashSet + Doubly-Linked List

```java
// LinkedHashSet extends HashSet, which uses LinkedHashMap internally
public class LinkedHashSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    public LinkedHashSet() {
        super(16, .75f, true);  // true = access-order (for LRU)
    }
}

// LinkedHashMap maintains:
// HashMap buckets + doubly-linked list through all entries
//   head → Entry1 ↔ Entry2 ↔ Entry3 → tail
// Iteration follows linked list order (insertion or access order)
```

### TreeMap — Red-Black Tree

```java
// OpenJDK TreeMap source (simplified)
public class TreeMap<K,V> implements NavigableMap<K,V> {
    private transient Entry<K,V> root;  // Red-black tree root
    private final Comparator<? super K> comparator;

    static final class Entry<K,V> {
        K key;
        V value;
        Entry<K,V> left;
        Entry<K,V> right;
        Entry<K,V> parent;
        boolean color = BLACK;
    }

    public V put(K key, V value) {
        Entry<K,V> t = root;
        if (t == null) {
            root = new Entry<>(key, value, null);
            size = 1;
            return null;
        }
        int cmp = compare(key, t.key);
        if (cmp < 0)      // go left
        else if (cmp > 0) // go right
        else              // key exists → update value
        // ... insert + balance (rotations + recoloring)
    }
}
```

**Red-Black Tree properties:**
1. Every node is red or black
2. Root is black
3. Red nodes have black children
4. Every path from root to leaf has same number of black nodes
5. Longest path ≤ 2× shortest path → balanced → O(log n)

```
TreeMap after inserting keys: 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80

              [50,B]
             /      \
        [30,B]      [70,B]
        /   \       /   \
    [20,R] [40,R] [60,R] [80,R]

In-order traversal: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 (sorted)
```

**TreeMap navigation methods (killer feature):**
```java
TreeMap<Integer, String> map = new TreeMap<>();
map.put(10, "A"); map.put(20, "B"); map.put(30, "C"); map.put(40, "D");

map.firstKey();           // 10
map.lastKey();            // 40
map.floorKey(25);         // 20 (greatest key ≤ 25)
map.ceilingKey(25);       // 30 (least key ≥ 25)
map.lowerKey(30);         // 20 (strictly less)
map.higherKey(30);        // 40 (strictly greater)
map.subMap(10, 30);       // {10=A, 20=B} (10 inclusive, 30 exclusive)
map.headMap(30);          // {10=A, 20=B}
map.tailMap(20);          // {20=B, 30=C, 40=D}
map.pollFirstEntry();     // removes and returns {10=A}
```

### PriorityQueue — Binary Min-Heap

```java
// OpenJDK PriorityQueue source (simplified)
public class PriorityQueue<E> {
    private transient Object[] queue;  // Binary heap in array
    private int size;
    private final Comparator<? super E> comparator;

    // Heap structure (min-heap):
    // Index:  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
    // Array: [10, 20, 15, 30, 25, 40, 35]
    //
    // Tree representation:
    //         10
    //        /  \
    //      20    15
    //     / \    /
    //   30  25  40
    //   /
    //  35
    //
    // Parent of i: (i-1)/2
    // Left child:  2*i + 1
    // Right child: 2*i + 2

    public boolean offer(E e) {
        if (size >= queue.length)
            grow(size + 1);
        siftUp(size, e);  // bubble up to maintain heap property
        size++;
        return true;
    }

    public E poll() {
        E result = (E) queue[0];  // root = min
        E moved = (E) queue[--size];
        queue[size] = null;
        if (size != 0)
            siftDown(0, moved);  // bubble down to maintain heap property
        return result;
    }
}
```

**PriorityQueue is NOT thread-safe.** Use `PriorityBlockingQueue` for concurrent scenarios.

## Section 3: Under the Hood

### HashSet equals/hashCode Contract in Action

```java
// What happens internally when you add to HashSet:
set.add(new User("Alice", 30));

// Step 1: compute hash = user.hashCode()
// Step 2: find bucket = hash & (table.length - 1)
// Step 3: traverse bucket, call equals() on each entry
// Step 4: if no equals() match → insert; if match → reject duplicate

// BROKEN: only override equals(), not hashCode()
class BadUser {
    String name;
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof BadUser && name.equals(((BadUser)o).name);
    }
    // hashCode() uses Object.hashCode() → identity-based
}
Set<BadUser> set = new HashSet<>();
set.add(new BadUser("Alice"));
set.add(new BadUser("Alice"));  // DUPLICATE! Different hash buckets
set.size();  // 2
```

### TreeSet with Comparator vs Comparable

```java
// Option 1: Element implements Comparable
class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    int salary;
    public int compareTo(Employee other) { return Integer.compare(salary, other.salary); }
}
TreeSet<Employee> set = new TreeSet<>();  // uses compareTo()

// Option 2: External Comparator
TreeSet<Employee> set = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Employee::getSalary));

// CRITICAL: TreeSet uses compareTo/Comparator, NOT equals()!
Employee e1 = new Employee(50000);
Employee e2 = new Employee(50000);
set.add(e1);
set.add(e2);
set.size();  // 1 if compareTo returns 0 (considered duplicate)
// BUT: e1.equals(e2) may still be false! Inconsistent with Set contract!
// Fix: ensure compareTo returns 0 iff equals() returns true
```

### PriorityQueue Iterator Does NOT Return Sorted Order

```java
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
pq.addAll(List.of(30, 10, 20, 50, 40));

pq.poll();  // 10 (heap order)
pq.poll();  // 20
pq.poll();  // 30

// BUT iteration is NOT sorted:
for (int n : pq) {
    System.out.println(n);  // Could print: 40, 50 (heap array order, NOT sorted!)
}
// To iterate in sorted order: repeatedly poll()
while (!pq.isEmpty()) System.out.println(pq.poll());
```

### LinkedHashMap Access-Order Mode (LRU Cache)

```java
// Access-order LinkedHashMap: get/put moves entry to tail
Map<String, byte[]> cache = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {
    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, byte[]> eldest) {
        return size() > MAX_CACHE_SIZE;
    }
};

// Access pattern:
cache.put("A", dataA);  // A
cache.put("B", dataB);  // A → B
cache.get("A");         // B → A (A moved to tail — most recently used)
cache.put("C", dataC);  // B → A → C
// If size > MAX: eldest (B) removed — least recently used
```

## Section 4: Production Use Cases

### Use Case 1: TreeMap for Time-Series Range Queries

```java
// Store metrics keyed by timestamp, query ranges efficiently
TreeMap<Instant, MetricSnapshot> metrics = new TreeMap<>();

// Insert
metrics.put(Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"), snapshot1);
metrics.put(Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:05:00Z"), snapshot2);

// Range query: all metrics between 10:00 and 10:30
NavigableMap<Instant, MetricSnapshot> range = metrics.subMap(
    Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"),
    true,  // inclusive
    Instant.parse("2024-01-15T10:30:00Z"),
    false  // exclusive
);
// O(log n + k) where k = results in range
```

### Use Case 2: PriorityQueue for Top-K Elements

```java
// Find top 10 highest-value transactions from 1 million records
public List<Transaction> topK(List<Transaction> transactions, int k) {
    // Min-heap of size k — O(n log k)
    PriorityQueue<Transaction> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(k,
        Comparator.comparing(Transaction::getAmount));

    for (Transaction tx : transactions) {
        minHeap.offer(tx);
        if (minHeap.size() > k)
            minHeap.poll();  // remove smallest of the heap
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(minHeap);
    // Alternative: stream().sorted().limit(k) is O(n log n) — worse for large n
}
```

### Use Case 3: HashSet for Deduplication in Data Pipeline

```java
// Deduplicate 10M event IDs before processing
Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(12_000_000);  // pre-size: 10M / 0.75 + 1
for (String eventId : eventStream) {
    if (!seen.add(eventId)) {  // add() returns false if duplicate
        duplicateCounter.increment();
        continue;
    }
    processEvent(eventId);
}
```

### Use Case 4: TreeSet for Scheduling

```java
// Task scheduler: always execute earliest-deadline task
TreeSet<Task> schedule = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparing(Task::getDeadline));

schedule.add(new Task("deploy", Instant.parse("2024-01-15T15:00:00Z")));
schedule.add(new Task("backup", Instant.parse("2024-01-15T14:00:00Z")));

Task next = schedule.pollFirst();  // backup (earliest deadline)
// O(log n) insert, O(log n) remove-min, always sorted
```

## Section 5: Performance Considerations

### Collection Performance Matrix

| Collection | add | remove | contains | iterate | sorted? | thread-safe? |
|-----------|-----|--------|----------|---------|---------|-------------|
| HashSet | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | O(n) | No | No |
| LinkedHashSet | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) | O(n) | Insertion order | No |
| TreeSet | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) | Yes | No |
| TreeMap | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) | Key-sorted | No |
| PriorityQueue | O(log n) | O(log n)* | O(n) | O(n) | Heap order | No |
| PriorityBlockingQueue | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) | O(n) | Heap order | Yes |

*poll() only — remove(Object) is O(n)

### When TreeMap Beats HashMap

```
Use TreeMap when you need:
  - Range queries (subMap, headMap, tailMap)
  - Floor/ceiling lookups (nearest key)
  - Sorted iteration
  - First/last key access

Use HashMap when you need:
  - Pure get/put/contains (no ordering)
  - Maximum throughput (O(1) vs O(log n))
  - Null keys (TreeMap rejects null keys)
```

### PriorityQueue vs TreeSet for Priority Access

```
PriorityQueue:
  + O(log n) offer/poll
  + O(1) peek
  - O(n) contains/remove arbitrary element
  - Iterator NOT sorted
  Best for: streaming top-K, task scheduling, Dijkstra's algorithm

TreeSet:
  + O(log n) all operations
  + Sorted iteration
  + NavigableSet (floor, ceiling, subSet)
  - No O(1) peek (but first() is O(log n))
  Best for: sorted unique elements with range queries
```

## Section 6: Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1: Using PriorityQueue Iterator Expecting Sorted Order

```java
// WRONG: iterator does not return elements in priority order
PriorityQueue<Task> pq = buildQueue();
for (Task t : pq) { process(t); }  // random heap order!

// RIGHT: poll until empty
while (!pq.isEmpty()) process(pq.poll());
```

### Mistake 2: Mutable Objects in HashSet/TreeSet

```java
Set<User> users = new HashSet<>();
User user = new User("Alice");
users.add(user);
user.setName("Bob");  // MUTATED after insertion!
users.contains(new User("Bob"));  // false — unfindable in HashSet
```

### Mistake 3: TreeSet Inconsistency Between compareTo and equals

```java
// compareTo returns 0 but equals returns false → violates Set contract
class Employee implements Comparable<Employee> {
    int id; int salary;
    public int compareTo(Employee o) { return Integer.compare(salary, o.salary); }
    // Two employees with same salary: compareTo=0 but equals=false
    // TreeSet keeps only one! Data loss!
}
// Fix: compare by unique field (id), or ensure consistency
```

### Mistake 4: Null in TreeMap/TreeSet

```java
TreeMap<String, Integer> map = new TreeMap<>();
map.put(null, 1);  // NullPointerException — null cannot be compared
// Use HashMap if null keys needed
```

### Mistake 5: Not Pre-Sizing HashSet

```java
// Same resize issue as HashMap — HashSet uses HashMap internally
Set<String> set = new HashSet<>(expectedSize * 4 / 3 + 1);
```

## Section 8: Tricky Follow-Up Questions

### FQ1: "Implement HashSet from scratch."

```java
class MyHashSet<E> {
    private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();
    private final HashMap<E, Object> map = new HashMap<>();

    public boolean add(E e) { return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null; }
    public boolean remove(E o) { return map.remove(o) == PRESENT; }
    public boolean contains(Object o) { return map.containsKey(o); }
    public int size() { return map.size(); }
}
```

### FQ2: "Can you use a custom object as TreeMap key without Comparable?"

Yes, provide a `Comparator` at construction: `new TreeMap<>(myComparator)`. The key class does not need to implement `Comparable`.

### FQ3: "What is the initial capacity of PriorityQueue?"

Default 11 (first prime above 10). Grows via `Arrays.copyOf` when full. Not related to heap property — just array sizing.

### FQ4: "How does LinkedHashSet maintain insertion order without slowing down HashSet operations?"

LinkedHashMap adds `before/after` pointers to each entry, forming a doubly-linked list alongside the hash table. Insert/remove in hash table is still O(1); linked list pointers updated in O(1). Iteration follows linked list: O(n) but O(1) per element.

### FQ5: "Design a data structure with insert, delete, getRandom all O(1)."

HashMap + ArrayList hybrid: HashMap stores element→index, ArrayList stores elements. Delete: swap deleted element with last, update HashMap, remove last from ArrayList. (LeetCode 380: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1))

## Section 9: Senior Engineer Answers

### A1: HashSet Internals

> "HashSet is a thin wrapper around HashMap — elements are stored as keys with a static dummy `PRESENT` object as value. This means all HashMap internals apply: hash function with spread bits, bucket array, linked list collision resolution, treeification at 8 nodes, 0.75 load factor with doubling resize. add() returns false if the key already exists (duplicate). The critical requirement is that elements must implement equals() and hashCode() consistently — equal objects must have the same hash code. I always use immutable objects or records as Set elements to prevent the subtle bug where mutating an element after insertion makes it unfindable."

### A2: Top-K with PriorityQueue

> "For finding top K elements from N items, I use a size-K min-heap (PriorityQueue). Iterate through all N elements: offer each into the heap, and if size exceeds K, poll the minimum. After processing all elements, the heap contains exactly the K largest. Time: O(N log K), Space: O(K). This is better than sorting all N elements (O(N log N)) when K is much smaller than N. For K=10 and N=10 million, that's 10M × log(10) ≈ 33M operations vs 10M × log(10M) ≈ 200M operations."

---

## Section 10: Technical Lead Answers

### A1: LRU Cache Architecture

> "I standardized our in-memory caching approach across services. For local JVM caches under 10K entries, we use Caffeine (which uses a variant of W-TinyLFU eviction — superior to LRU). For custom LRU needs, I provided a `LinkedHashMap` template with access-order and `removeEldestEntry()`. The ADR explicitly banned unbounded HashMap caches — three production OOMs traced to caches without eviction. For distributed caching, we use Redis with TTL. The key architectural decision: cache keys must be immutable records, cache values must be serializable, and every cache must expose hit/miss/eviction metrics via Micrometer. This reduced cache-related incidents by 95% and improved average cache hit rate from 72% to 91% through proper sizing and eviction policies."

## Section 11: Real Production Incident Examples

### Incident 1: TreeSet compareTo/equals Inconsistency

**Company:** HR platform (Workday-scale)  
**Symptom:** Employee records silently dropped during deduplication  
**Root Cause:** `Employee.compareTo()` compared by salary, but `equals()` compared by employee ID. Two employees with same salary: TreeSet kept only one.

**Fix:** Changed `compareTo` to compare by unique employee ID. Added unit test asserting `compareTo(a,b)==0 iff equals(a,b)`.

---

### Incident 2: PriorityQueue OOM in Task Scheduler

**Company:** Cloud platform (AWS-scale)  
**Symptom:** Scheduler pod OOMKilled after 6 hours  
**Root Cause:** `PriorityQueue<Task>` accumulated tasks without polling. Failed tasks were re-offered but never removed. Queue grew to 2M entries.

**Fix:** Bounded queue with max size + dead-letter queue for failed tasks. Added metric alert on queue depth > 10K.

## Section 12: Revision Notes

### Must-Know Facts

```
HashSet = HashMap keys + PRESENT dummy value
LinkedHashSet = LinkedHashMap (insertion/access order)
TreeSet = TreeMap keys only (red-black tree, sorted)
TreeMap = red-black tree, O(log n), NavigableMap (floor/ceiling/subMap)
PriorityQueue = binary min-heap in array, O(log n) offer/poll, NOT sorted iteration

HashSet: one null allowed, no order, O(1)
TreeSet: no null, sorted, O(log n), uses compareTo NOT equals
PriorityQueue: no null, heap order, poll() returns min (or Comparator-defined)

LRU Cache: LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) + removeEldestEntry()
Top-K: size-K min-heap, O(N log K)

Keys in HashSet/TreeMap: MUST be immutable
TreeSet: compareTo=0 must match equals()=true
```

## Chapter 10: Immutable Objects and Functional Programming

> **Reading Time:** ~50 minutes | **Page Equivalent:** ~20 pages  
> **Prerequisites:** Chapters 06–09  
> **Interview Weight:** ★★★★☆

---

## Section 1: Beginner Explanation

### What Is Immutability?

An immutable object is one whose state cannot be changed after construction. All fields are final, no setters, and if the object contains mutable references (like a List), those are defensively copied.

```java
// MUTABLE — state can change
public class MutableUser {
    private String name;
    public void setName(String name) { this.name = name; }
}

// IMMUTABLE — state frozen at construction
public final class ImmutableUser {
    private final String name;
    private final List<String> roles;

    public ImmutableUser(String name, List<String> roles) {
        this.name = name;
        this.roles = List.copyOf(roles);  // defensive copy
    }
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public List<String> getRoles() { return roles; }  // unmodifiable
}
```

**Why immutability matters:**
- **Thread safety** — no synchronization needed, freely shared across threads
- **HashMap/HashSet keys** — hash code never changes
- **Defensive copying** — callers cannot corrupt internal state
- **Caching** — safe to cache, no stale data
- **Reasoning** — easier to understand code behavior

### What Is Functional Programming in Java?

Java 8+ added functional programming features while remaining an object-oriented language:

```java
// IMPERATIVE (how to do it)
List<String> result = new ArrayList<>();
for (String name : names) {
    if (name.startsWith("A")) {
        result.add(name.toUpperCase());
    }
}

// FUNCTIONAL (what to do)
List<String> result = names.stream()
    .filter(name -> name.startsWith("A"))
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
```

**Core functional concepts in Java:**
| Concept | Java Feature |
|---------|-------------|
| First-class functions | Lambda expressions, method references |
| Pure functions | Stateless lambdas, no side effects |
| Immutability | `final`, records, `List.of()` |
| Higher-order functions | Functions accepting/returning functions |
| Declarative style | Streams API |

---

## Section 2: Internal Working

### Creating Truly Immutable Classes

```java
// The 5 rules for immutable classes:
// 1. Class is final (prevent subclass mutation)
// 2. All fields are private and final
// 3. No setters
// 4. Defensive copy of mutable inputs
// 5. Defensive copy of mutable outputs (or return unmodifiable views)

public final class Money {
    private final String currency;
    private final BigDecimal amount;

    public Money(String currency, BigDecimal amount) {
        this.currency = Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
        this.amount = Objects.requireNonNull(amount);
    }

    // "Modification" creates NEW instance (persistent data structure)
    public Money add(Money other) {
        if (!this.currency.equals(other.currency))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Currency mismatch");
        return new Money(currency, amount.add(other.amount));
    }

    public String getCurrency() { return currency; }
    public BigDecimal getAmount() { return amount; }
}
```

### Java Records (Java 16+) — Built-In Immutability

```java
// Record: compiler generates constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, toString
public record UserDto(Long id, String name, String email) {
    // Compact constructor for validation
    public UserDto {
        Objects.requireNonNull(name, "name required");
        Objects.requireNonNull(email, "email required");
    }

    // Can add methods
    public String displayName() {
        return name + " <" + email + ">";
    }
}

// Compiler generates:
// - private final fields: id, name, email
// - public constructor UserDto(Long id, String name, String email)
// - public Long id(), String name(), String email()  (no get prefix!)
// - equals(), hashCode(), toString()
// - Class is final
```

### Functional Interfaces

```java
// Built-in functional interfaces (java.util.function):
@FunctionalInterface
interface Predicate<T>      { boolean test(T t); }
@FunctionalInterface
interface Function<T,R>     { R apply(T t); }
@FunctionalInterface
interface Consumer<T>       { void accept(T t); }
@FunctionalInterface
interface Supplier<T>       { T get(); }
@FunctionalInterface
interface BiFunction<T,U,R> { R apply(T t, U u); }
@FunctionalInterface
interface UnaryOperator<T>  { T apply(T t); }  // extends Function<T,T>

// Custom functional interface:
@FunctionalInterface
public interface Validator<T> {
    ValidationResult validate(T input);
    // default and static methods allowed — doesn't break functional interface
}
```

### Lambda Expression Internals

```java
// Lambda
Comparator<String> comp = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length();

// Compiled to:
// 1. invokedynamic bytecode instruction
// 2. Bootstrap method: LambdaMetafactory.metafactory()
// 3. Generates synthetic class: MyClass$$Lambda$1/0x0000000800c00000
// 4. Synthetic class implements Comparator, calls the lambda body

// Equivalent anonymous class (OLD way — creates .class file per lambda):
Comparator<String> comp = new Comparator<String>() {
    public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.length() - b.length(); }
};
// Lambda is preferred: no extra .class per instance, better performance
```

### Method References

```java
// Four types of method references:
Class::staticMethod       // Integer::parseInt
instance::instanceMethod  // str::length (bound)
Class::instanceMethod     // String::length (unbound)
Class::new                // ArrayList::new (constructor)

// Examples:
list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase)           // unbound instance
list.forEach(System.out::println)                   // bound instance
stream.map(Integer::parseInt)                     // static
list.stream().collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new))  // constructor
```

## Section 3: Under the Hood

### String Immutability — The Canonical Example

```java
// String is immutable — every "modification" creates a new object
String s = "Hello";
s.concat(" World");  // Returns NEW string "Hello World"
System.out.println(s);  // Still "Hello" — original unchanged

// Why String is immutable:
// 1. String pool safety — "Hello" in pool cannot be changed by any reference
// 2. Thread safety — freely shared without synchronization
// 3. hashCode caching — computed once, cached (String.hash field)
// 4. Security — class names, file paths, URLs cannot be modified after validation
```

**String concatenation under the hood:**
```java
// Java 8: compiles to StringBuilder chain
String result = "Hello" + name + "!";
// → new StringBuilder().append("Hello").append(name).append("!").toString()
// 3 objects created: StringBuilder, intermediate, final String

// Java 9+: invokedynamic with StringConcatFactory
// → JVM optimizes concatenation strategy at runtime
// → May use byte[], char[], or Vector (SIMD) based on pattern
```

### Immutable Collections Internals (Java 9+)

```java
List<String> list = List.of("A", "B", "C");

// Internal: NOT ArrayList!
// - Object array with exact size (no capacity field)
// - Class: ImmutableCollections$List12 (for ≤2 elements, specialized)
// - add/remove/set → UnsupportedOperationException
// - null elements → NullPointerException at creation
// - Iterator: no modCount check (truly immutable, no CME possible)
// - Memory: ~40 bytes for 3 strings vs ~80+ for ArrayList
```

### Defensive Copying Patterns

```java
// WRONG: exposes internal mutable state
public class Team {
    private final List<String> members = new ArrayList<>();
    public List<String> getMembers() { return members; }  // caller can modify!
}

// RIGHT: defensive copy on input AND output
public class Team {
    private final List<String> members;

    public Team(List<String> members) {
        this.members = List.copyOf(members);  // defensive copy IN
    }
    public List<String> getMembers() {
        return members;  // already immutable via List.copyOf
    }
}
```

### Persistent Data Structures Concept

```java
// Functional "modification" returns new instance, original unchanged
Money balance = new Money("USD", new BigDecimal("1000"));
Money afterDeposit = balance.add(new Money("USD", new BigDecimal("500")));
// balance is still $1000
// afterDeposit is $1500
// Both can be safely shared across threads

// Java doesn't have built-in persistent collections (unlike Clojure/Scala)
// But Guava's ImmutableList/ImmutableMap provide similar guarantees:
ImmutableList<String> list = ImmutableList.of("A", "B");
// list.add("C"); → UnsupportedOperationException
```

## Section 4: Production Use Cases

### Use Case 1: Immutable DTOs for API Responses

```java
// API response — immutable by design
public record OrderResponse(
    Long orderId,
    String status,
    BigDecimal total,
    List<OrderItemResponse> items
) {
    public OrderResponse {
        items = List.copyOf(items);  // defensive copy of mutable list
    }
}
// Safe to cache, safe to pass between threads, safe as HashMap key
```

### Use Case 2: Functional Error Handling (Railway-Oriented)

```java
// Chain validations without nested if-else
public ValidationResult validateOrder(Order order) {
    return validateNotNull(order)
        .andThen(o -> validatePositiveAmount(o.getAmount()))
        .andThen(o -> validateValidCurrency(o.getCurrency()))
        .andThen(o -> validateInventory(o.getProductId(), o.getQuantity()));
}

@FunctionalInterface
interface ValidationStep<T> {
    ValidationResult apply(T input);
    default ValidationStep<T> andThen(ValidationStep<T> next) {
        return input -> {
            ValidationResult result = this.apply(input);
            return result.isValid() ? next.apply(input) : result;
        };
    }
}
```

### Use Case 3: Strategy Pattern with Lambdas

```java
// Replace class-per-strategy with functional approach
Map<String, Function<Transaction, BigDecimal>> feeCalculators = Map.of(
    "STANDARD", tx -> tx.getAmount().multiply(new BigDecimal("0.01")),
    "PREMIUM",  tx -> tx.getAmount().multiply(new BigDecimal("0.005")),
    "VIP",      tx -> BigDecimal.ZERO
);

BigDecimal fee = feeCalculators
    .getOrDefault(customer.getTier(), feeCalculators.get("STANDARD"))
    .apply(transaction);
```

### Use Case 4: Immutable Configuration Objects

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")
public record AppConfig(
    String serviceName,
    Duration timeout,
    int maxRetries,
    List<String> allowedOrigins
) {
    public AppConfig {
        allowedOrigins = List.copyOf(allowedOrigins);
    }
}
// Spring binds properties → immutable config
// Safe to inject anywhere without defensive copying
```

## Section 5: Performance Considerations

### Immutability Performance Trade-offs

| Aspect | Mutable | Immutable |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| Object creation | Reuse same object | New object per "change" |
| GC pressure | Lower (fewer objects) | Higher (more short-lived objects) |
| Thread safety cost | Synchronization/Locks | Zero (free sharing) |
| Memory | Single copy | Multiple versions coexist |
| Correctness | Error-prone | Safer by construction |

**When immutability hurts:** High-frequency updates to large objects (e.g., game state updated 60fps). Use mutable buffers internally, publish immutable snapshots.

**When immutability wins:** DTOs, config, cache keys, shared state, concurrent pipelines.

### Lambda vs Anonymous Class Performance

```
Benchmark: 10M invocations
Anonymous class:  450ms (separate .class, class loading overhead)
Lambda:           380ms (invokedynamic, synthetic class cached)
Method reference:   370ms (slightly faster — no lambda body)
Direct call:        50ms (baseline)
```

### Auto-Boxing in Functional Code

```java
// BAD: boxing in stream
IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
    .mapToObj(i -> process(i))  // int → Integer boxing
    .collect(Collectors.toList());

// GOOD: stay primitive
IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000)
    .forEach(i -> process(i));  // no boxing
```

## Section 6: Common Mistakes

### Mistake 1: Shallow Immutability

```java
public final class ImmutableConfig {
    private final List<String> servers;  // final reference
    public ImmutableConfig(List<String> servers) {
        this.servers = servers;  // BUG: stores caller's mutable list!
    }
}
// Caller: config.getServers().add("evil.com"); — mutates "immutable" object
// Fix: this.servers = List.copyOf(servers);
```

### Mistake 2: Mutable Date Fields in "Immutable" Classes

```java
public final class Event {
    private final Date timestamp;  // Date is MUTABLE!
    public Event(Date timestamp) { this.timestamp = timestamp; }
    // Caller: event.getTimestamp().setTime(0); — mutated!
    // Fix: use Instant (immutable) or copy: new Date(timestamp.getTime())
}
```

### Mistake 3: Non-Deterministic Lambdas in Parallel Streams

```java
// BUG: parallel stream with shared mutable state
List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
IntStream.range(0, 1000).parallel().forEach(result::add);
// ArrayList is NOT thread-safe → data loss/corruption!

// Fix: collect (thread-safe reduction)
List<Integer> result = IntStream.range(0, 1000).parallel()
    .boxed().collect(Collectors.toList());
```

### Mistake 4: Using Function Where Predicate Expected

```java
// filter() expects Predicate (returns boolean)
list.stream().filter(s -> s.length());  // COMPILE ERROR — int not boolean
list.stream().filter(s -> s.length() > 0);  // Correct
```

### Mistake 5: Records with Mutable Components

```java
public record Team(String name, List<String> members) {}
// members list is mutable! Caller can modify after construction
Team team = new Team("Alpha", new ArrayList<>(List.of("Alice")));
team.members().add("Eve");  // MUTABLE despite record!
// Fix: compact constructor with List.copyOf(members)
```

## Section 8: Tricky Follow-Up Questions

### FQ1: "Is Integer immutable? What about autoboxing?"

`Integer` is immutable. But `int` primitive is mutable (it's on the stack). Autoboxing creates new `Integer` objects (except -128 to 127 which are cached). `Integer i = 1; i += 1;` creates a new Integer(2) object — the original Integer(1) is unchanged.

### FQ2: "Can you make a mutable class immutable after construction?"

Not truly. You can freeze modifications by removing setters and returning unmodifiable views, but if someone holds a reference to the mutable internals before freezing, they can still modify. True immutability requires immutable construction from the start.

### FQ3: "What is the difference between `final` and immutable?"

`final` means the reference cannot be reassigned. The object it points to can still be mutated. `List<String> list = List.of("A")` — final reference to an immutable object. `final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>()` — final reference to a mutable object (contents can change).

### FQ4: "How does Guava's ImmutableList differ from List.of()?"

Both are truly immutable. Guava's versions work on Java 8+, support slightly more operations (e.g., `ImmutableList.copyOf()` with better null handling), and have builder patterns. `List.of()` is Java 9+ native, lighter weight, but rejects null elements.

### FQ5: "Can lambdas capture local variables? What are the restrictions?"

Yes, but only effectively final variables. The lambda captures a copy of the value, not the variable itself. Reassigning the variable after the lambda is created causes a compile error.

## Section 9: Senior Engineer Answers

### A1: Immutability

> "An immutable object cannot change state after construction. I achieve this with final fields, no setters, defensive copying of mutable inputs and outputs, and a final class to prevent subclass mutation. Since Java 16, I use records for DTOs — the compiler generates immutable boilerplate. The key benefits are thread safety without synchronization, safe use as HashMap keys, and easier reasoning about code. The trade-off is creating new objects for every change, which increases GC pressure. For high-churn data like game state, I use mutable internals with immutable published snapshots. For DTOs, config, and cache keys, immutability is non-negotiable."

### A2: Functional Programming in Java

> "Java 8 brought functional programming via lambda expressions, method references, and the Streams API. Lambdas compile to invokedynamic with LambdaMetafactory — no .class file per lambda unlike anonymous classes. I use functional style for collection processing (filter/map/reduce), strategy pattern replacement (Map of String to Function), and callback APIs (CompletableFuture.thenApply). I avoid parallel streams in production unless I've verified thread safety of the entire pipeline — the common bug is shared mutable state in forEach. My rule: streams for readability in business logic, traditional loops for performance-critical hot paths where allocation matters."

---

## Section 10: Technical Lead Answers

### A1: Immutability Standards

> "I mandated immutability for all DTOs, API responses, configuration objects, and cache keys across our 80-service fleet. The catalyst was a production incident where a mutable cache key was modified after insertion, causing 30% cache misses. The standard: 1) All DTOs must be Java records or Lombok @Value. 2) No public setters on domain objects passed between layers. 3) ArchUnit tests enforce these rules. 4) All HashMap/ConcurrentHashMap keys must be records. 5) Defensive copying enforced via List.copyOf() in constructors. This eliminated an entire class of concurrency bugs and cache corruption issues. The team initially resisted due to 'more object creation,' but GC profiling showed the overhead was negligible (<1% allocation increase) compared to the correctness benefits."
