**Business metrics dashboard:** Rides/hour heatmap by geohash, supply/demand ratio, driver utilization (time on trip / time online).

### Production Incident Example

*Uber 2016 surge pricing backlash during Sydney hostage crisis:* Automated surge algorithm raised prices during emergency demand spike. Lesson: manual override capability for ops team; geofenced surge caps; ethical guardrails in pricing engine with human-in-the-loop for anomalies > 2× baseline.

---

## Section 10: Common Mistakes & Trade-offs

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---------|-------------|
| Global driver search | Latency and data transfer impossible at scale |
| MySQL for location updates | 750K writes/sec exceeds single-node capacity |
| Synchronous matching in API request | Timeout if matching takes > 30 sec; use async + WebSocket |
| No driver lock during offer | Two rides assigned to same driver |
| Storing all location history in PostgreSQL | 75 GB/day bloat; use Cassandra |
| Ignoring driver acceptance rate | Drivers game system by accepting then cancelling |

**Matching strategies:**

| Strategy | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| Greedy (nearest driver) | Fast, simple | Suboptimal global utilization |
| Batch matching (30 sec window) | Optimal assignment (Hungarian algo) | Higher rider wait |
| Stackelberg (surge first, then match) | Revenue optimized | Complex |

Uber uses greedy with batched optimization in high-density areas.

### Deep Dive: Geospatial Indexing Alternatives

| Structure | Query Time | Update Time | Best For |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|----------|
| Redis GEO (geohash) | O(log N + K) | O(log N) | < 100K drivers/city |
| QuadTree | O(log N + K) | O(log N) | In-memory, single city |
| H3 (Uber's hex grid) | O(1) cell lookup | O(1) | Surge pricing, demand heatmaps |
| PostGIS (R-tree) | O(log N + K) | O(log N) | Complex polygon queries |

**Uber H3:** Uber open-sourced H3 — a hexagonal hierarchical geospatial index. Each hex cell has a resolution (0–15). Drivers assigned to hex cell at resolution 7 (~1.2 km²). Surge calculated per cell. Matching queries adjacent cells (k-ring) for driver search. Mention H3 in Uber interviews — it signals you've researched their stack.

### Deep Dive: ETA Calculation Pipeline

```
Driver location update (every 4 sec)
  → Kafka location.updates
  → ETA Service (consumes, maintains road graph cache)
  → Pre-computed: distance matrix for top 1000 (origin_hex, dest_hex) pairs
  → On-demand: OSRM API call for uncommon routes (cached 5 min)
  → ETA stored in Redis: eta:{driverId}:{pickupHex} → minutes
```

ETA accuracy is a competitive differentiator. Factors: real-time traffic (Google/HERE API), historical patterns (ML model per city per hour), driver speed profile. Goldman Sachs parallel: ETA is like trade execution latency — measure, optimize, alert on regression.

### Deep Dive: Payment Integration

Trip completion triggers payment asynchronously:

```
TRIP_COMPLETED event → Payment Service
  → Calculate final fare (actual distance × rate × surge at trip start)
  → Charge rider (pre-auth at request time, capture at completion)
  → Credit driver (minus platform commission)
  → Handle tip (optional, separate transaction)
```

Pre-authorization at ride request: hold 1.5× estimated fare on rider's card. Capture actual at completion. Release difference. If actual > hold, attempt additional charge. Idempotency key = trip_id for all payment operations.

### Tricky Follow-Up Questions

**"Rider requests ride in SF, driver is in Oakland — do you match?"**  
Configurable max matching radius (default 5 km, expand to 15 km). Cross-bay bridge trips have longer ETA — ranking algorithm penalizes ETA > 10 min. Surge in SF may not apply to Oakland driver (different hex cell). Geographic boundaries matter for pricing and matching.

**"How do you handle drivers gaming the system (position spoofing)?**  
GPS validation: speed plausibility (reject teleportation), accelerometer cross-check on mobile, historical route consistency. Flagged drivers get manual review. Rate acceptance algorithm: drivers with < 50% acceptance deprioritized in matching.

### Technical Lead Answer Framing

> "Uber's core challenge is geographic partitioning — every algorithm must be city-scoped. I'd never design a global driver search. The trip state machine in PostgreSQL is the source of truth for money and accountability; Redis geo index is ephemeral and rebuildable. As a lead, I'd define the matching SLA (time-to-match p99 < 30 sec) and build the observability to measure it per city per hour. Surge pricing needs a manual override — automated pricing during emergencies is a reputational risk we learned the hard way."

---

## Section 11: Interview Questions & Answers

**Q1: How do you find the nearest driver in < 1 second?**  
Geohash-partitioned Redis Geo index. `GEORADIUS` on cell-specific key returns 20 nearest in O(log N). Filter by status/type, rank by ETA from cached routing. All in-memory — sub-10 ms. No database query on hot path.

**Q2: 750K location updates per second — how?**  
Kafka partitioned by driverId geohash. 100+ stateless Location Service consumers. Redis Geo updated asynchronously. Batch `GEOADD` commands (pipeline 100 updates). Location is ephemeral — no durable DB write unless driver on active trip.

**Q3: Prevent two riders matching the same driver?**  
Distributed lock: `SETNX driver:{id}:lock {tripId} EX 15`. Only offer ride if lock acquired. On accept, lock converts to `active_trip`. On reject/timeout, release lock. PostgreSQL optimistic lock on trip row as second layer.

**Q4: How does surge pricing work?**  
Every 2 min, compute demand/supply ratio per geohash cell from Kafka event counts. Multiplier = f(ratio), capped at 3×. Stored in Redis. Fare estimate reads multiplier at request time. Decouple from matching — surge affects price, not match priority (unless configured).

**Q5: Design trip tracking for rider in real-time.**  
Driver location → Kafka → Trip Service → rider's WebSocket connection. Update every 4 sec. Cassandra stores trail for dispute resolution. ETA recalculated every 30 sec. If WebSocket drops, rider polls `GET /rides/{id}` every 5 sec as fallback.

---

## Section 12: Revision Notes

- **15M rides/day ≈ 175/sec**; peak 875/sec per mega-city
- **750K location updates/sec** → Kafka + Redis Geo, not SQL
- **Geohash-partitioned** Redis `GEORADIUS` for nearest driver
- **Trip state machine** in PostgreSQL with optimistic locking
- **Dispatch:** top 3 drivers, 15 sec timeout, expand radius on failure
- **Surge:** demand/supply ratio per cell, recalculated every 2 min
- **Geographic isolation:** each city = independent dispatch domain
- **Driver lock** (`SETNX`) prevents double assignment
- **Location trail** in Cassandra; ephemeral index in Redis
- **ETA:** routing service with cache; fallback to straight-line × 1.3

## Section 1: Problem Statement & Requirements

### What We Are Building

A global video-on-demand (VOD) streaming platform serving movies and TV shows to 200M+ subscribers. Users browse a catalog, receive personalized recommendations, and stream video with adaptive bitrate (ABR) — quality adjusts to network conditions. No live streaming in scope.

### Functional Requirements

| # | Requirement | Priority |
|---|-------------|----------|
| F1 | Browse catalog (search, categories, detail pages) | Must |
| F2 | Stream video with adaptive quality (360p–4K) | Must |
| F3 | Resume playback from last position | Must |
| F4 | Personalized homepage recommendations | Must |
| F5 | Multi-device profiles per account | Must |
| F6 | Subtitles and audio tracks in multiple languages | Must |
| F7 | Download for offline viewing | Should |
| F8 | Content rating and parental controls | Should |

### Non-Functional Requirements

| NFR | Target |
|-----|--------|
| Video start time | < 2 sec (p99) |
| Rebuffering ratio | < 0.5% of playback time |
| Availability | 99.99% |
| Scale | 200M subscribers, 1B hours/month viewed |
| Global reach | 190+ countries |
| Concurrent streams | 15M peak |

### Out of Scope

- Live streaming / sports
- Content production / encoding pipeline internals (touched briefly)
- Billing / subscription management

## Section 2: Capacity Estimation

```
VIEWING
  1B hours/month ÷ 30 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 385K concurrent streams average
  Peak (prime time, 3×) ≈ 15M concurrent streams

BANDWIDTH (dominant cost)
  Average bitrate (ABR): 5 Mbps
  15M streams × 5 Mbps = 75 Tbps peak egress
  → Requires global CDN (Open Connect / CloudFront); never serve from origin

STORAGE
  Catalog: 15,000 titles
  Encodings per title: ~120 variants (resolutions × bitrates × codecs × audio)
  Avg file size per variant chunk (2-sec segment): 1 MB
  2-hour movie: ~3600 segments × 120 variants × 1 MB ≈ 432 GB per title
  Total: 15K × 432 GB ≈ 6.5 PB (with dedup across shared encodings: ~3 PB)

METADATA
  Per title: ~10 KB (title, cast, genres, ratings, artwork URLs)
  15K × 10 KB = 150 MB — trivial, lives in cache

VIEWING HISTORY / RESUME
  200M users × 50 active titles × 100 bytes = 1 GB
  Writes: 200M users seeking/pausing → ~50K writes/sec peak
```

### Extended Capacity: CDN Egress Economics

```
75 Tbps peak egress:
  Commercial CDN (CloudFront): ~$0.02/GB → ~$2M/day at full load
  Open Connect (self-operated): hardware amortization ~$200K/day
  → 10× cost advantage at Netflix scale

Per-subscriber bandwidth:
  1B hours/month ÷ 200M subscribers = 5 hours/month average
  5 hours × 5 Mbps × 3600 sec = 9 GB/month per subscriber
  200M × 9 GB = 1.8 EB/month total (theoretical max)

Encoding compute:
  15K titles × 120 variants × 2 hours × 30 min encode
  = 15K × 120 × 0.5 hours = 900K compute-hours per catalog refresh
  Spot instances at $0.01/hr = $9K per full re-encode
```

### Extended Capacity: Recommendation Pre-Computation

```
200M profiles × 10 rows × 50 titles/row = 100B recommendation entries
  Storage: 100B × 20 bytes (profile_id, row, rank, title_id, score) = 2 TB
  Spark job: 200M profiles × 50ms inference = 10M seconds = 115 hours serial
  With 1000-node Spark cluster: ~7 minutes per batch run
  Runs every 6 hours; stale recommendations acceptable for browse
```

---

## Section 3: API Design

### Catalog APIs

```http
GET  /api/v1/browse/homepage?profileId={id}     # personalized rows
GET  /api/v1/titles/{titleId}                    # detail page
GET  /api/v1/search?q={query}&profileId={id}
GET  /api/v1/titles/{titleId}/similar
```

### Playback APIs

```http
GET  /api/v1/play/{titleId}?profileId={id}
     → returns manifest URL + DRM license endpoint

POST /api/v1/playback/events
     { "titleId", "profileId", "event": "START|PROGRESS|PAUSE|END",
       "positionSec": 3600, "quality": "1080p", "bitrate": 5000 }
```

### Homepage Response

```json
{
  "rows": [
    {
      "title": "Trending Now",
      "titles": [
        {"titleId": "t_80192098", "name": "Stranger Things", "thumbnail": "https://cdn.../thumb.jpg", "match": 98}
      ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Because you watched Dark",
      "titles": [...]
    }
  ]
}
```

### Streaming Protocol

Uses **MPEG-DASH** or **HLS** (HTTP Live Streaming):

```
GET https://cdn.netflix.com/title_80192098/manifest.mpd
→ XML manifest listing all quality variants

GET https://cdn.netflix.com/title_80192098/1080p/segment_0042.ts
→ 2-second video chunk (actual media bytes)
```

Client ABR algorithm (buffer-based): monitor buffer level → switch quality up/down without rebuffering.

## Section 4: Database Design

### Content Metadata — Cassandra + Elasticsearch

```sql
-- Cassandra: title metadata (key-value, high read)
CREATE TABLE titles (
    title_id    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT,
    type        TEXT,       -- MOVIE, SERIES
    genres      SET<TEXT>,
    cast        LIST<TEXT>,
    rating      TEXT,
    duration_sec INT,
    release_year INT,
    artwork     MAP<TEXT, TEXT>  -- size → URL
);
```

Elasticsearch for full-text search across title names, cast, descriptions.

### Viewing Progress — Cassandra

```sql
CREATE TABLE viewing_progress (
    profile_id   UUID,
    title_id     TEXT,
    position_sec INT,
    updated_at   TIMESTAMP,
    device_id    TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (profile_id, title_id)
);
```

Write on every pause/seek/end (debounced to every 30 sec during playback to reduce writes).

### Recommendations — Pre-computed Store

```sql
-- Cassandra: pre-computed recommendation rows
CREATE TABLE recommendations (
    profile_id  UUID,
    row_type    TEXT,     -- TRENDING, BECAUSE_YOU_WATCHED, TOP_PICKS
    rank        INT,
    title_id    TEXT,
    score       FLOAT,
    PRIMARY KEY (profile_id, row_type, rank)
);
```

Generated offline by ML pipeline (Spark) every 6 hours. Serving is pure read — no ML inference on request path.

### Encoding Metadata — PostgreSQL

```sql
CREATE TABLE encoding_variants (
    title_id     TEXT,
    variant_id   TEXT,     -- 1080p_h264_5000k
    resolution   TEXT,
    codec        TEXT,
    bitrate_kbps INT,
    cdn_path     TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (title_id, variant_id)
);
```

### Playback Analytics — Kafka → Data Lake

Events: start, progress (every 30s), quality switch, rebuffer, end. Consumed by data warehouse for ML training and QoS monitoring.

## Section 5: High-Level Design

```
┌──────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│  TV / Mobile │────▶│ API Gateway │────▶│  Catalog Service │
│  Web Client  │     └─────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘
└──────┬───────┘                                  │
       │                                          ▼
       │ direct CDN                          ┌─────────────┐
       │ (video bytes)                       │ Cassandra / │
       ▼                                     │ Elasticsearch│
┌──────────────────┐                         └─────────────┘
│  Open Connect    │
│  CDN (1000+ PoPs)│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  ┌────────────┐  │     │         Control Plane              │
│  │ ISP Edge   │  │     │  ┌───────────┐  ┌───────────────┐ │
│  │ Appliances │  │     │  │Recommend. │  │ Encoding      │ │
│  └────────────┘  │     │  │ Service   │  │ Pipeline      │ │
└──────────────────┘     │  └─────┬─────┘  └───────┬───────┘ │
                         │        │                │         │
                         │  ┌─────▼─────┐  ┌───────▼───────┐ │
                         │  │ ML Batch  │  │ S3 Origin     │ │
                         │  │ (Spark)   │  │ (mezzanine)   │ │
                         │  └───────────┘  └───────────────┘ │
                         └─────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Playback Flow

1. User clicks Play → Client calls `GET /play/{titleId}`
2. Playback Service:
   - Checks entitlement (subscription active, geo-restriction)
   - Fetches viewing progress from Cassandra (resume position)
   - Returns signed CDN manifest URL (time-limited token, 4-hour expiry)
   - Returns DRM license server URL (Widevine/FairPlay)
3. Client fetches manifest from **nearest CDN PoP** (not origin)
4. ABR engine selects initial quality based on bandwidth estimate
5. Client downloads 2-sec segments sequentially from CDN
6. Every 30 sec: POST playback progress event (async, non-blocking)
7. On quality switch: ABR adjusts without interrupting playback

### Content Ingestion Pipeline (Offline)

```
Studio delivers mezzanine (4K master)
  → S3 origin storage
  → Encoding farm (AWS Spot instances): FFmpeg → 120 variants
  → Packaged as DASH/HLS segments
  → Replicated to all CDN PoPs (Open Connect appliances)
  → Metadata written to Cassandra + Elasticsearch
  → Thumbnails generated, uploaded to CDN
```

Encoding is **embarrassingly parallel** — 1000+ EC2 Spot instances per title. A 2-hour movie encodes in ~30 min wall-clock with sufficient parallelism.

---

## Section 6: Low-Level Design

### Signed CDN URL Generation

```java
public String generatePlaybackUrl(String titleId, String profileId) {
    String cdnPath = "/titles/" + titleId + "/manifest.mpd";
    long expiry = Instant.now().getEpochSecond() + 14400; // 4 hours
    String token = hmacSha256(CDN_SECRET, cdnPath + expiry + profileId);
    return CDN_BASE + cdnPath + "?exp=" + expiry + "&token=" + token + "&profile=" + profileId;
}
```

CDN edge validates HMAC before serving. Prevents hotlinking and unauthorized access.

### Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) — Client Algorithm (Simplified)

```
Buffer-based ABR (Netflix uses proprietary + BOLA family):
  buffer_level = seconds_of_video_buffered

  if buffer_level > 30 sec AND bandwidth > current_bitrate × 1.5:
      switch_up()
  if buffer_level < 10 sec OR bandwidth < current_bitrate × 0.8:
      switch_down()
  if buffer_level < 2 sec:
      rebuffer_event() → switch_down_aggressively()
```

Server provides 10–15 quality ladder rungs (240p to 4K). Client never requests quality server doesn't have.

### Recommendation Serving

```java
public HomepageResponse getHomepage(UUID profileId) {
    // All pre-computed — no ML at request time
    List<RecommendationRow> rows = cassandraRepo
        .getRecommendations(profileId, List.of("TRENDING", "TOP_PICKS", "CONTINUE_WATCHING", "BECAUSE_YOU_WATCHED"));

    // Enrich with title metadata from local cache (Caffeine, 15K titles fits in memory)
    return enrichWithMetadata(rows);
}
```

**Continue Watching** row: join `viewing_progress` with title metadata. Updated in real-time (not batch).

### DRM (Digital Rights Management)

Widevine (Android/Chrome), FairPlay (iOS/Safari), PlayReady (Edge). License server validates entitlement → issues decryption key. Encrypted segments served from CDN; decryption happens client-side in hardware TEE (Trusted Execution Environment).

---

## Section 7: Scaling Strategies

| Layer | Strategy |
|-------|----------|
| Video delivery | CDN at ISP edge (Open Connect); 95%+ cache hit; origin never touched during playback |
| API services | Stateless microservices; auto-scale on CPU/request rate |
| Cassandra | Partition by profile_id (recommendations) and title_id (metadata) |
| Search | Elasticsearch cluster with 3 replicas; index per region |
| Encoding | Spot instances; priority queue; encode popular titles first |
| Recommendations | Pre-compute offline; serve from Cassandra (no inference latency) |
| Viewing progress | Debounce writes (30 sec); Cassandra handles 50K writes/sec |

**Netflix Open Connect:** Custom CDN appliances installed inside ISP data centers. Content pre-positioned based on predicted demand (ML-driven). 1000+ appliances globally serve 75 Tbps without touching public internet backbone for last mile.

**Multi-region:** Active-active API in 3 regions (US, EU, APAC). Cassandra multi-DC. CDN is inherently distributed. Catalog metadata replicated globally; viewing progress is region-local with async cross-region sync.

---

## Section 8: Failure Handling

| Failure | Mitigation |
|---------|------------|
| CDN PoP down | Client redirects to next-nearest PoP (anycast DNS); multi-CDN fallback |
| Origin unavailable | CDN serves from cache (content pre-positioned); no user impact if cache warm |
| ABR quality drop | Client switches to lower bitrate; user sees lower quality, not rebuffer |
| Recommendation service down | Serve generic trending row (hardcoded fallback); degrade gracefully |
| Cassandra write failure (progress) | Client retries; local cache preserves position; sync on recovery |
| DRM license server down | Playback cannot start; show error with retry; pre-warm license on play click |
| Encoding pipeline delay | Title not available until encoding completes; show "coming soon" |
| Entitlement check failure | Default deny; never serve content without valid subscription |

**Chaos engineering:** Netflix Simian Army (Chaos Monkey, Chaos Kong) randomly kills production instances. Streaming must survive zone-level failures.

**Stale recommendations:** Pre-computed every 6 hours. Stale up to 6 hours acceptable. Continue Watching is real-time (separate table, not batch).

---

## Section 9: Monitoring & Observability

| Metric | Threshold | Business Impact |
|--------|-----------|-----------------|
| Video start time p99 | > 3 sec | User abandonment |
| Rebuffer ratio | > 1% | Poor QoE; churn risk |
| CDN cache hit ratio | < 90% | Origin overload; cost spike |
| Manifest fetch latency | > 500 ms | Delayed start |
| ABR quality distribution | Monitor | Detect CDN throttling |
| Encoding queue depth | > 100 titles | Content delay |
| Playback error rate | > 0.5% | DRM or CDN issue |
| API p99 latency (homepage) | > 500 ms | Browse experience degraded |

**Per-title QoS dashboard:** Start time, rebuffer rate, average quality per title per region. Detect bad encodes or CDN placement issues.

**Client-side beacons:** Player reports QoS metrics every 30 sec to Kafka. Real User Monitoring (RUM) for actual experience, not synthetic.

### Production Incident Example

*Netflix Christmas Eve 2012 AWS outage:* Single AZ failure in US-East took down critical services. Led to multi-AZ mandate, Chaos Monkey development, and eventual migration away from single-region dependency. Lesson: no single point of failure; CDN must serve cached content even when all APIs are down (playback continues if manifest already fetched).

---

## Section 10: Common Mistakes & Trade-offs

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---------|-------------|
| Serving video from origin | 75 Tbps impossible from central servers; CDN is mandatory |
| ML inference on homepage request | 200ms+ latency per row; pre-compute instead |
| Writing viewing progress every second | 15M writes/sec; debounce to 30 sec |
| Single encoding quality | Users on slow networks rebuffer constantly; ABR required |
| No DRM | Content piracy; studio licensing agreements violated |
| Storing video in database | BLOB storage is anti-pattern; object storage + CDN |

**Encoding trade-off:**

| Approach | Pros | Cons |
|----------|------|------|
| Pre-encode all qualities | Instant playback start | 120× storage per title |
| Transcode on-the-fly | Storage efficient | CPU expensive; start delay |
| Per-title optimization (per-shot encoding) | 20% bandwidth savings | Complex pipeline (Netflix approach) |

### Deep Dive: Open Connect CDN Architecture

Netflix's Open Connect is not a traditional CDN — it is a **content delivery network operated as a partnership with ISPs:**

```
Content flow:
  Origin (AWS S3) → Netflix encoding → Open Connect Appliance (OCA)
  OCA installed inside ISP data center (free for ISP)
  95%+ of Netflix traffic never leaves ISP network

Appliance specs:
  - 100+ TB storage per appliance
  - Serves 40 Gbps per appliance
  - Pre-positioned content based on ML demand prediction
  - Manifests still served from API (control plane)
```

**Why this matters in interviews:** Netflix's bandwidth cost is a fraction of what AWS CloudFront would charge at 75 Tbps because they own the last mile. The trade-off: capital expense of hardware vs operational expense of commercial CDN. For a startup, use CloudFront/Akamai; at Netflix scale, build Open Connect.

### Deep Dive: Content Discovery & A/B Testing

Netflix runs 250+ A/B tests simultaneously on the homepage. Architecture:

```
User request → Experiment Service (assigns variant from cache)
  → Variant A: row order algorithm v1
  → Variant B: row order algorithm v2
  → Both serve from same pre-computed Cassandra recommendations
  → Different row ordering / thumbnail selection only
  → Metrics: start rate, completion rate, hours viewed → Kafka → analysis
```

Experiment assignment cached per user (sticky for 30 days). No ML retraining per experiment — only presentation layer changes. This is how Netflix innovates without risking playback infrastructure.

### Deep Dive: Multi-Profile & Parental Controls

```
Account (billing entity)
  └── Profile 1 (adult) — independent recommendations, viewing history
  └── Profile 2 (kids) — content filter by rating (PG, PG-13)
  └── Profile 3 (adult) — separate continue-watching

profile_id is the key for:
  - viewing_progress table
  - recommendations table
  - playback events
  - parental control settings
```

Kids profile: hard filter at API layer — `GET /play/{titleId}` checks content rating against profile's max rating. Encoding pipeline tags every title with rating metadata.

### Tricky Follow-Up Questions

**"How do you handle a user watching on two devices simultaneously?"**  
Netflix allows 2–4 concurrent streams depending on plan. On play request: check active stream count for account (Redis counter). If at limit, return 403 with message. Each playback event has `deviceId` — deduplicate counting. Stream ends on 30 sec inactivity or explicit stop event.

**"Design for live sports streaming (extension)."**  
Live differs from VOD: single encoding pipeline (no 120 variants pre-encoded), chunked via LL-HLS (1-sec segments), origin serves directly (no pre-positioning), higher rebuffer tolerance, DRM more aggressive. CDN switches from pull (VOD) to push (live origin → CDN edge). Mention this to show breadth.

### Technical Lead Answer Framing

> "Netflix architecture has two completely separate planes: the control plane (APIs, recommendations, metadata) and the data plane (CDN video delivery). I'd never let video bytes touch application servers. The key Technical Lead decision is pre-computation vs real-time: recommendations, encodings, and CDN placement are all batch/offline. Only 'Continue Watching' and playback authorization are real-time. I'd define QoS SLOs (start time, rebuffer ratio) measured from client beacons, not server metrics — the user's player experience is the truth."

---

## Section 11: Interview Questions & Answers

**Q1: How do you serve 15M concurrent video streams?**  
CDN at ISP edge (Open Connect). Video bytes never touch API servers. Client downloads 2-sec segments from nearest PoP via HTTP. 75 Tbps distributed across 1000+ appliances. API only serves manifest URL (few KB) and DRM license.

**Q2: Explain adaptive bitrate streaming.**  
Content encoded at 10–15 quality levels (240p–4K). Manifest lists all variants. Client ABR algorithm monitors buffer level and bandwidth → selects appropriate quality. Switches seamlessly between segments. Buffer-based: switch up when buffer > 30 sec, down when < 10 sec.

**Q3: How do recommendations work at 200M user scale?**  
Offline batch ML (Spark): collaborative filtering + content-based + deep learning (Netflix's approach). Pre-compute top-N per profile per row type every 6 hours. Store in Cassandra. Homepage API is pure read — p99 < 50 ms. No inference on request path.

**Q4: How do you handle resume playback across devices?**  
`viewing_progress` table keyed by (profile_id, title_id). Updated on pause/end (debounced during playback). Any device fetches same row on play. Conflict: last-write-wins (latest timestamp). Netflix syncs within 30 sec.

**Q5: Design the encoding pipeline for a new title.**  
Mezzanine to S3 → job queue (SQS/Kafka) → encoding workers (FFmpeg on Spot instances) → 120 variants → package as DASH/HLS → replicate to CDN PoPs → update metadata in Cassandra. Parallelize across instances; 2-hour movie in ~30 min. Priority queue: popular/new titles first.

---

## Section 12: Revision Notes

- **75 Tbps peak** → CDN mandatory; API servers never serve video bytes
- **ABR (DASH/HLS):** 2-sec segments; client switches quality based on buffer
- **Open Connect:** CDN appliances inside ISP data centers
- **Recommendations:** pre-computed offline (Spark); served from Cassandra
- **Viewing progress:** debounced writes (30 sec); Cassandra (profile_id, title_id)
- **DRM:** Widevine/FairPlay; license server validates entitlement
- **Signed CDN URLs:** HMAC token prevents hotlinking
- **Encoding:** 120 variants per title; Spot instances; ~30 min per movie
- **Start time < 2 sec:** manifest from CDN + pre-positioned content
- **Chaos engineering:** zone failures must not stop playback (CDN cache)

## Section 1: Requirements & Capacity Estimation

### Functional Requirements

| # | Requirement |
|---|-------------|
| F1 | Upload videos (up to 12 hours, 256 GB) |
| F2 | Stream with adaptive bitrate (shared with Netflix model) |
| F3 | Search videos by title, tags, channel |
| F4 | Subscribe to channels; personalized feed |
| F5 | Like, comment, share; view counts |
| F6 | Live streaming (basic) |
| F7 | Monetization (ads, Super Chat) |

### Non-Functional Requirements

| NFR | Target |
|-----|--------|
| Upload | Support 500 hours/minute of new content |
| View start time | < 2 sec |
| Availability | 99.99% |
| Scale | 2B MAU, 1B hours/day watched |

### Capacity Estimation

```
UPLOADS
  500 hours/min × 60 × 24 = 720K hours/day new content
  Avg 500 MB/hour → 360 PB/day raw upload
  Transcoded to ~5 qualities → ~1.8 EB/day (deduplicated via CDN placement)

VIEWS
  1B hours/day ÷ 24 ≈ 42M concurrent streams average
  Peak: ~120M concurrent × 3 Mbps avg = 360 Tbps (CDN)

METADATA
  800M videos × 2 KB metadata = 1.6 TB
  Comments: 1B/day × 200 bytes = 200 GB/day
  View counts: 5B views/day → counter service, not per-row UPDATE

WRITES
  View count increments: 5B/day ≈ 58K/sec → counter service (not SQL UPDATE)
  Comments: 100M/day ≈ 1,160/sec → Cassandra
  Uploads: 500 hrs/min ≈ 8.3/sec → async pipeline
```

**Key difference from Netflix:** User-generated content (UGC) — unpredictable upload volume, viral videos, social features (comments, subscriptions).

## Section 2: Design (APIs, Database, HLD, LLD)

### Core APIs

```http
POST /api/v1/videos/upload          # initiate resumable upload (GCS/S3)
POST /api/v1/videos/{id}/process    # trigger transcoding
GET  /api/v1/videos/{id}/manifest    # playback manifest (signed CDN URL)
GET  /api/v1/feed?userId={id}        # personalized home feed
GET  /api/v1/search?q={query}
POST /api/v1/videos/{id}/view         # increment view (debounced)
POST /api/v1/videos/{id}/comments
POST /api/v1/channels/{id}/subscribe
```

### Database Design

| Data | Store | Key |
|------|-------|-----|
| Video metadata | PostgreSQL / Bigtable | video_id |
| View counts | Redis counter + periodic flush to DB | video_id |
| Comments | Cassandra (partition by video_id) | video_id + timestamp |
| Subscriptions | Cassandra (partition by user_id) | user_id + channel_id |
| Feed | Pre-computed (fan-out on write for < 1M subscribers; fan-out on read for celebrities) | user_id |
| Search index | Elasticsearch | inverted index |
| Video blobs | GCS/S3 + CDN | object key |

```sql
-- Video metadata
CREATE TABLE videos (
    video_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    channel_id   BIGINT,
    title        TEXT,
    description  TEXT,
    status       TEXT,    -- UPLOADING, PROCESSING, READY, DELETED
    duration_sec INT,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);

-- View count (denormalized, updated via counter service)
ALTER TABLE videos ADD COLUMN view_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0;
```

### High-Level Design

```
┌──────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Client  │────▶│ API Gateway │────▶│  Upload Service  │──▶ GCS (resumable)
└────┬─────┘     └─────────────┘     └──────────────────┘
     │                                          │
     │ CDN (video)                              ▼
     ▼                                 ┌──────────────────┐
┌──────────────┐                      │ Transcoding Farm │
│ CDN (video   │                      │ (FFmpeg, GPU)    │
│  segments)   │                      └────────┬─────────┘
└──────────────┘                               ▼
     ▲                                 ┌──────────────────┐
     │                                 │ Metadata Service │
┌────┴─────┐     ┌─────────────┐      │ + Search Index   │
│ Feed Svc │◀───│ Subscription │      └──────────────────┘
└──────────┘     │ Graph Svc   │
                 └─────────────┘
```

### Key LLD Patterns

**Resumable upload:** Client uploads chunks to GCS directly (pre-signed URL). On completion, publish `video.uploaded` to Kafka → transcoding pipeline.

**View count (approximate):** Client debounces view event (30 sec watch threshold). Redis `INCR view:{videoId}`. Flush to PostgreSQL every 5 min. Display rounded count ("1.2M views"). Exact count unnecessary.

**Feed generation (hybrid fan-out):**
- Regular channels (< 100K subs): fan-out on write — on upload, push video_id to each subscriber's feed cache
- Celebrity channels (MrBeast): fan-out on read — merge subscribed channels at read time
- Threshold at 100K subscribers

**Viral video handling:** CDN auto-scales; origin shield caches hot content. Transcoding prioritizes videos with rising view velocity.

---

## Section 3: Scaling & Failure Handling

### Scaling

| Component | Strategy |
|-----------|----------|
| Video delivery | Global CDN; same as Netflix (ABR, DASH/HLS) |
| Uploads | Direct-to-GCS; resumable; no API server in data path |
| Transcoding | GPU fleet (NVIDIA); priority queue by predicted popularity |
| View counts | Redis HyperLogLog or counter; never SQL UPDATE per view |
| Comments | Cassandra; partition by video_id |
| Search | Elasticsearch with sharding; index updated async |
| Feed | Redis sorted sets per user; TTL 7 days |

### Failure Handling

| Failure | Mitigation |
|---------|------------|
| Upload interrupted | Resumable upload protocol (GCS resumable API) |
| Transcoding fails | Retry 3×; alert creator; status = FAILED |
| CDN miss on viral video | Origin shield; pre-warm based on view velocity |
| View count Redis loss | Rebuild from event log; approximate acceptable |
| Celebrity upload (50M subs fan-out) | Async fan-out via Kafka; feed populated over minutes |
| Comment spam | Rate limit; ML moderation pipeline |

---

## Section 4: Interview Questions & Answers

**Q1: How is YouTube different from Netflix architecturally?**  
UGC vs professional content. YouTube has uploads (write-heavy), social graph (subscriptions, comments), and unpredictable virality. Netflix is read-heavy with curated catalog. YouTube needs fan-out feed, counter service, and resumable uploads. Netflix needs recommendation ML and encoding pipeline — overlap on CDN/ABR streaming.

**Q2: How do you count views without overloading the database?**  
Redis counter per video_id. Client sends view event after 30 sec watch. `INCR` in Redis (58K/sec easily handled). Flush to DB every 5 min in batch. Display approximate count. HyperLogLog for unique viewers if needed.

**Q3: Design the upload pipeline.**  
Client gets pre-signed GCS URL → uploads directly (resumable, chunked). On complete, Kafka event triggers transcoding farm (GPU FFmpeg). Output: multiple quality DASH/HLS segments → CDN. Metadata written to PostgreSQL. Search index updated async. Status: UPLOADING → PROCESSING → READY.

**Q4: How do you build the subscription feed?**  
Hybrid fan-out. Regular channels: on upload, Kafka fan-out writes video_id to each subscriber's Redis feed (sorted set by timestamp). Celebrity channels (> 100K subs): fan-out on read — fetch recent videos from subscribed channels at request time, merge, sort, cache 5 min.

**Q5: A video goes viral — 10M views in 1 hour. What happens?**  
CDN handles traffic (auto-scale). View counter in Redis handles 10M INCR. If single Redis key hot: shard counter (video_id % N). Transcoding already complete. Comments may lag (Cassandra scales). Feed fan-out for creator's subscribers already done at upload. Origin shield prevents CDN stampede.

---

## Section 5: Revision Notes

- **UGC platform:** uploads + social graph + unpredictable virality
- **500 hrs/min upload** → direct-to-GCS resumable; async transcoding
- **View counts:** Redis INCR, not SQL UPDATE; approximate display
- **Feed:** fan-out on write (< 100K subs); fan-out on read (celebrities)
- **Comments:** Cassandra partitioned by video_id
- **CDN + ABR** same as Netflix for playback delivery
- **Search:** Elasticsearch with async index updates
- **360 Tbps peak** → CDN mandatory; origin shield for viral content

> **Interview Weight:** ★★★★★ (Goldman Sachs, Amazon, Stripe — correctness > scale)

## Section 1: Problem Statement & Requirements

### What We Are Building

A payment processing platform handling money movement between users, merchants, and banks. Supports payment authorization, capture, refund, and settlement. Think Stripe or Goldman Sachs internal payments rail — correctness and auditability trump raw throughput.

### Functional Requirements

| # | Requirement | Priority |
|---|-------------|----------|
| F1 | Process payment (authorize + capture) for a purchase | Must |
| F2 | Refund (full or partial) | Must |
| F3 | Idempotent payment processing (retry-safe) | Must |
| F4 | Payment status inquiry | Must |
| F5 | Support multiple payment methods (card, bank transfer, wallet) | Must |
| F6 | Merchant settlement (batch payout) | Must |
| F7 | PCI DSS compliance (no raw card storage) | Must |
| F8 | Multi-currency with FX conversion | Should |
| F9 | Recurring/subscription payments | Should |

### Non-Functional Requirements

| NFR | Target |
|-----|--------|
| Correctness | Exactly-once money movement (no double charge, no lost funds) |
| Availability | 99.999% (financial systems standard) |
| Latency | p99 < 3 sec for card authorization |
| Durability | Zero data loss; full audit trail |
| Throughput | 10K transactions/sec peak |
| Compliance | PCI DSS Level 1, SOX, GDPR |

### Out of Scope

- Fraud detection ML model internals (reference as separate service)
- Cryptocurrency payments
- Check/wire manual processing

---

## Section 2: Capacity Estimation

```
TRANSACTIONS
  100M transactions/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,160 TPS average
  Peak (Black Friday, 10×) ≈ 10K TPS

STORAGE
  Per transaction record: ~1 KB (ids, amounts, status, timestamps, metadata)
  Audit log entry: ~500 bytes
  100M/day × 1.5 KB × 365 × 7 years ≈ 380 TB (regulatory retention)
  Hot data (90 days): ~13 TB

BANDWIDTH
  API requests: 10K TPS × 2 KB = 20 MB/sec — modest
  Dominated by batch settlement file transfers to banks (nightly, SFTP)

EXTERNAL CALLS
  Card network (Visa/MC): ~500 ms per authorization
  At 10K TPS: need 5,000 concurrent connections to payment gateway
  Connection pooling + async I/O essential
```

### Extended Capacity: Settlement Batch Processing

```
End-of-day settlement (T+1):
  100M transactions/day batched into settlement files
  File format: NACHA (ACH), ISO 20022 (wire), proprietary (card networks)
  Generated at 2 AM; transmitted via SFTP to bank by 4 AM
  Settlement file size: 100M × 200 bytes = 20 GB
  Processing time: 30 min on dedicated settlement worker

Reconciliation:
  Bank returns confirmation file next morning
  Compare 100M entries: hash-based diff in ~10 min
  Discrepancy rate target: < 0.001% (1000 per 100M)
```

### Extended Capacity: Connection Pool to Payment Gateway

```
At 10K TPS with 500ms gateway latency:
  Concurrent connections needed = 10,000 × 0.5 = 5,000
  Pool config: min=500, max=5000, idle timeout=30s
  Circuit breaker: open after 5 failures in 10 sec
  Fallback: queue requests for 2 sec; reject after timeout

Gateway rate limits (Visa):
  ~1,000 TPS per merchant ID
  Solution: multiple merchant IDs (MID) with round-robin
  Or: payment aggregator (Stripe) handles MID pooling
```

## Section 3: API Design

### Payment APIs

```http
POST /api/v1/payments                    # create payment (authorize)
POST /api/v1/payments/{id}/capture       # capture authorized amount
POST /api/v1/payments/{id}/refund        # full or partial refund
GET  /api/v1/payments/{id}               # status inquiry
GET  /api/v1/payments?merchantId={id}&from={date}&to={date}
```

### Create Payment

```http
POST /api/v1/payments
Idempotency-Key: uuid-v4-unique-per-attempt
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "merchantId": "merch_abc123",
  "amount": {"value": 4999, "currency": "USD"},   // cents
  "paymentMethod": {
    "type": "CARD",
    "token": "tok_visa_4242"    // tokenized — never raw PAN
  },
  "description": "Order #12345",
  "metadata": {"orderId": "ord_12345"}
}

Response 201:
{
  "paymentId": "pay_8f3a2b1c",
  "status": "AUTHORIZED",
  "amount": {"value": 4999, "currency": "USD"},
  "createdAt": "2026-06-14T10:00:00Z",
  "idempotencyKey": "uuid-v4-unique-per-attempt"
}
```

### Payment Status State Machine

```
CREATED → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED → SETTLED
              │            │
              ▼            ▼
          DECLINED     REFUNDED (partial or full)
              │
              ▼
          FAILED
```

### Webhook (Merchant Notification)

```http
POST https://merchant.com/webhooks/payments
X-Signature: hmac_sha256(payload, merchant_secret)

{
  "event": "payment.captured",
  "paymentId": "pay_8f3a2b1c",
  "amount": {"value": 4999, "currency": "USD"},
  "timestamp": "2026-06-14T10:00:05Z"
}
```

## Section 4: Database Design

### Ledger — Double-Entry Bookkeeping (PostgreSQL)

**Never update balances directly.** Every money movement is an immutable ledger entry.

```sql
CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    transaction_id UUID NOT NULL,
    account_id     UUID NOT NULL,       -- user, merchant, platform, bank
    entry_type     TEXT NOT NULL,       -- DEBIT, CREDIT
    amount_cents   BIGINT NOT NULL,     -- always positive
    currency       CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    description    TEXT
);
-- INVARIANT: for every transaction_id, SUM(debits) = SUM(credits)

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id       UUID NOT NULL,
    account_type   TEXT NOT NULL,       -- USER, MERCHANT, PLATFORM, SUSPENSE
    currency       CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

-- Balance is COMPUTED, never stored (or cached with reconciliation)
CREATE VIEW account_balances AS
SELECT account_id, currency,
    SUM(CASE WHEN entry_type='CREDIT' THEN amount_cents ELSE -amount_cents END) AS balance_cents
FROM ledger_entries GROUP BY account_id, currency;
```

### Payment Records

```sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    idempotency_key  UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    merchant_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    amount_cents     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    currency         CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status           TEXT NOT NULL,
    payment_method   JSONB,
    external_ref     TEXT,          -- card network transaction ID
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ,
    updated_at       TIMESTAMPTZ,
    version          INT DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_merchant ON payments(merchant_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_idempotency ON payments(idempotency_key);
```

### Idempotency Store — Redis + PostgreSQL

```
Redis: idempotency:{key} → {paymentId, status, response_body} TTL 24h
PostgreSQL: UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_key (permanent dedup)
```

### Audit Log — Append-Only (Immutable)

```sql
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    log_id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    entity_type    TEXT,
    entity_id      UUID,
    action         TEXT,
    actor          TEXT,
    old_state      JSONB,
    new_state      JSONB,
    ip_address     INET,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
-- No UPDATE or DELETE allowed; enforced by DB permissions
```

## Section 5: High-Level Design

```
┌──────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Merchant    │────▶│ API Gateway │────▶│  Payment Service │
│  App / POS   │     │ + Idempotency│     │  (orchestrator)  │
└──────────────┘     └─────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘
                                                   │
                    ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                    │              │               │                │
                    ▼              ▼               ▼                ▼
            ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌────────────┐
            │ Ledger   │  │ Payment      │  │ Fraud    │  │ Payment    │
            │ Service  │  │ Gateway      │  │ Service  │  │ Method     │
            │ (ACID)   │  │ (Visa/MC/    │  │ (risk    │  │ Vault      │
            └────┬─────┘  │  ACH)        │  │  score)  │  │ (tokenize) │
                 │        └──────────────┘  └──────────┘  └────────────┘
                 ▼
            ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
            │PostgreSQL│     │    Kafka     │     │ Settlement   │
            │ (ledger, │     │  (events)    │     │ Service      │
            │ payments)│     └──────┬───────┘     │ (batch/night) │
            └──────────┘            │             └──────────────┘
                                    ▼
                           ┌──────────────┐
                           │ Webhook      │
                           │ Dispatcher   │
                           └──────────────┘
```

### Payment Authorization Flow

1. Merchant sends `POST /payments` with `Idempotency-Key`
2. API Gateway checks Redis idempotency cache → if exists, return cached response
3. Payment Service:
   a. Creates payment record (status=CREATED) in PostgreSQL
   b. Calls Fraud Service → risk score < threshold? continue : DECLINED
   c. Calls Payment Gateway (Visa/MC network) → authorize card
   d. **Within single DB transaction:**
      - Update payment status → AUTHORIZED
      - Insert ledger entries: DEBIT user account, CREDIT suspense account
   e. Publish `payment.authorized` to Kafka
4. Return 201 to merchant
5. Webhook Dispatcher notifies merchant asynchronously

### Capture Flow (Separate Step — Two-Phase)

```
Authorization: hold funds (merchant ships later)
Capture: actually move funds (merchant confirms shipment)
```

1. `POST /payments/{id}/capture`
2. Payment Service calls gateway capture API
3. DB transaction: status → CAPTURED; move from suspense to merchant account in ledger
4. Publish `payment.captured` → webhook

**Why two-phase:** E-commerce authorizes at checkout, captures at shipment. Prevents charging for cancelled orders.

### Refund Flow

1. `POST /payments/{id}/refund` with `amount` (partial allowed)
2. Validate: refund_amount ≤ captured_amount - previous_refunds
3. Call gateway refund API
4. DB transaction: ledger entries reverse (DEBIT merchant, CREDIT user)
5. Status → REFUNDED (or PARTIALLY_REFUNDED)

## Section 6: Low-Level Design

### Idempotent Payment Processing

```java
@Transactional
public PaymentResponse processPayment(PaymentRequest req, UUID idempotencyKey) {
    // Step 1: Check idempotency (DB unique constraint is ultimate guard)
    Optional<Payment> existing = paymentRepo.findByIdempotencyKey(idempotencyKey);
    if (existing.isPresent()) {
        return toResponse(existing.get()); // same response as original
    }

    // Step 2: Create payment record
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(new Payment(req, idempotencyKey, CREATED));

    // Step 3: External authorization (outside transaction — with compensation)
    GatewayResponse gwResponse;
    try {
        gwResponse = paymentGateway.authorize(req.getPaymentMethod(), req.getAmount());
    } catch (GatewayTimeoutException e) {
        payment.setStatus(FAILED);
        paymentRepo.save(payment);
        throw new PaymentException("Gateway timeout", e);
    }

    // Step 4: Atomic ledger + status update
    if (gwResponse.isApproved()) {
        ledgerService.recordTransaction(payment.getId(), List.of(
            new Entry(req.getUserAccount(), DEBIT, req.getAmount()),
            new Entry(SUSPENSE_ACCOUNT, CREDIT, req.getAmount())
        ));
        payment.setStatus(AUTHORIZED);
        payment.setExternalRef(gwResponse.getTransactionId());
    } else {
        payment.setStatus(DECLINED);
    }
    paymentRepo.save(payment);

    // Step 5: Cache idempotency response
    idempotencyCache.set(idempotencyKey, toResponse(payment), 24h);
    eventPublisher.publish(new PaymentAuthorizedEvent(payment));
    return toResponse(payment);
}
```

### Ledger Service — Double-Entry Invariant

```java
@Transactional(isolation = SERIALIZABLE)
public void recordTransaction(UUID txnId, List<Entry> entries) {
    long totalDebits = entries.stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getType() == DEBIT).mapToLong(Entry::getAmount).sum();
    long totalCredits = entries.stream()
        .filter(e -> e.getType() == CREDIT).mapToLong(Entry::getAmount).sum();

    if (totalDebits != totalCredits) {
        throw new LedgerInvariantViolationException(txnId);
    }

    entries.forEach(e -> ledgerRepo.insert(txnId, e));
    // Never UPDATE or DELETE ledger entries — append only
}
```

### Handling Gateway Timeout (Critical Edge Case)

```
Scenario: We send authorize to Visa, Visa approves, but our connection times out.
We don't know the outcome.

Resolution:
1. Payment status = PENDING_UNKNOWN
2. Reconciliation worker queries gateway by external_ref (if we got one) or by idempotency key
3. If approved: complete ledger entries, status → AUTHORIZED
4. If declined/not found: status → FAILED
5. Never retry authorization without checking — risk of double charge
```

### Reconciliation (Nightly Batch)

```java
@Scheduled(cron = "0 2 * * *") // 2 AM daily
public void reconcile() {
    // Compare our ledger with bank settlement files (SFTP)
    List<Discrepancy> diffs = compare(ourLedger, bankSettlementFile);
    diffs.forEach(d -> {
        if (d.isAmountMismatch()) alertFinanceTeam(d);
        if (d.isMissingInBank()) retrySettlement(d);
        if (d.isMissingInLedger()) createAdjustingEntry(d);
    });
}
```

## Section 7: Scaling Strategies

| Component | Strategy |
|-----------|----------|
| Payment Service | Horizontal; stateless; partition by merchant_id |
| PostgreSQL ledger | Partition by month; read replicas for reporting; SERIALIZABLE for writes |
| Idempotency cache | Redis cluster; 24h TTL |
| Payment Gateway calls | Async I/O (WebClient); connection pool 5000; circuit breaker |
| Kafka events | Partition by payment_id; consumers for webhooks, analytics, settlement |
| Settlement | Batch processing at night; not on critical path |

**10K TPS on PostgreSQL:** Achievable with connection pooling (PgBouncer), partitioned tables, and optimized indexes. Goldman Sachs uses specialized ledger databases (e.g., custom append-only stores) for higher throughput. For interview: PostgreSQL with partitioning handles 10K TPS; mention event sourcing for 100K+.

**Multi-region:** Active-passive (not active-active for ledger). Primary region handles writes; DR region has read replica with < 1 sec lag. Failover promotes replica. **Never dual-write to two ledger databases** — split-brain causes money duplication.

---

## Section 8: Failure Handling

| Failure | Mitigation |
|---------|------------|
| Gateway timeout | Status = PENDING_UNKNOWN; reconciliation worker resolves |
| Double charge (retry) | Idempotency key dedup at API + DB unique constraint |
| Ledger write fails after gateway approve | Compensation: void/cancel authorization at gateway |
| Kafka down | Payment still completes (DB is source of truth); events replayed from outbox |
| PostgreSQL failover | Synchronous replication; RPO = 0; automatic promotion |
| Partial refund exceeds captured | Validate in application + DB CHECK constraint |
| Webhook delivery fails | Retry 3× with exponential backoff; dead letter queue; merchant polls API |
| Fraud service down | Configurable: fail-open (approve with flag) or fail-closed (decline) |

**Saga pattern for distributed payment:**

```
Authorize (local TX) → Capture (local TX) → Settlement (batch)
  │ compensation: void authorization
  │ compensation: refund capture
```

Each step is independently compensatable. No 2PC across payment gateway and our DB.

**Outbox pattern:** Write payment event to `outbox` table in same DB transaction as ledger. Separate poller publishes to Kafka. Guarantees at-least-once event delivery without dual-write problem.

---

## Section 9: Monitoring & Observability

| Metric | Threshold |
|--------|-----------|
| Payment success rate | < 99.5% |
| Authorization latency p99 | > 3 sec |
| Gateway timeout rate | > 0.1% |
| Idempotency cache hit rate | Monitor (high = client retries) |
| Ledger invariant violations | > 0 (P0 alert — should never happen) |
| Reconciliation discrepancies | > 0 daily |
| Webhook delivery success rate | < 99% |
| PENDING_UNKNOWN count | > 100 (stuck payments) |

**Financial audit dashboard:** Total volume, success/decline/fraud ratio, average ticket size, settlement lag, currency breakdown.

**Alerting hierarchy:**
- P0: Ledger invariant violation, double-entry mismatch
- P1: Gateway down, reconciliation failure
- P2: Elevated decline rate, webhook delivery failures

### Production Incident Example

*Stripe double-charge incident pattern:* Client retries `POST /payments` without idempotency key on network timeout. Server processes both → double charge. Fix: enforce `Idempotency-Key` header (return 400 without it); DB unique constraint; return same response for duplicate key. Goldman lesson: idempotency is not optional in payment APIs — it is the contract.

---

## Section 10: Common Mistakes & Trade-offs

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---------|-------------|
| Storing raw card numbers (PAN) | PCI DSS violation; massive fine; breach liability |
| Updating balance column directly | Race conditions; money created or destroyed |
| Retrying gateway call without idempotency | Double charge |
| Synchronous webhook in payment flow | Merchant downtime blocks payments |
| Single-phase (auth+capture combined) | Cannot cancel before shipment |
| Active-active multi-region ledger | Split-brain → duplicate funds |
| No reconciliation | Silent money leaks discovered months later |

**Consistency vs availability trade-off:**

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| Ledger writes | CP (consistent + partition-tolerant) | Money correctness > availability |
| Payment status reads | Can be eventually consistent | Stale status for 1 sec acceptable |
| Fraud check | Fail-closed at Goldman; fail-open at startups | Risk appetite |

### Deep Dive: PCI DSS Compliance Architecture

```
Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) — isolated network segment:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Payment Method Vault (tokenization)    │
  │  - Raw PAN enters here ONLY             │
  │  - Returns token: tok_visa_4242         │
  │  - PAN never stored in Payment Service  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │ token only
         ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Payment Service (out of PCI scope)   │
  │  - Processes tokens only              │
  │  - No raw card data                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Scope reduction:** By tokenizing at the edge (Stripe Elements, Braintree hosted fields), the merchant's payment service never touches PAN — PCI scope shrinks from Level 1 to SAQ A (self-assessment). Goldman builds its own vault (full PCI Level 1 audit annually). For interviews: always mention tokenization to reduce PCI scope.

### Deep Dive: Multi-Currency & FX

```json
{
  "amount": {"value": 4999, "currency": "EUR"},
  "settlementCurrency": "USD",
  "fxRate": 1.0850,
  "settlementAmount": {"value": 5423, "currency": "USD"}
}
```

FX rate locked at authorization time (not capture). Stored in payment record. Settlement uses locked rate. FX provider (Reuters, internal desk) called once per authorization. Rounding rules: always round in customer's favor for display, banker's rounding for ledger.

### Deep Dive: Event Sourcing for Audit (Goldman Pattern)

At Goldman Sachs scale, the ledger is an event stream:

```
Event: PaymentAuthorized { paymentId, amount, accounts, timestamp }
Event: PaymentCaptured { paymentId, captureAmount, timestamp }
Event: PaymentRefunded { paymentId, refundAmount, reason, timestamp }

Projection: account_balances (materialized view, rebuilt from events)
Projection: payment_status (materialized view)

Audit: complete event log retained 7 years (regulatory)
```

Benefits: perfect audit trail (every state change recorded), replay capability, temporal queries ("what was balance at 2025-12-31?"). Trade-off: complexity vs query performance. CQRS separates write (event log) from read (projections).

### Deep Dive: Fraud Detection Integration

```
Payment request → Fraud Service (synchronous, < 100 ms)
  Inputs: amount, velocity (orders/hour), device fingerprint, IP geo,
          merchant category, card BIN, historical chargeback rate
  Output: risk_score (0-100), decision (APPROVE, REVIEW, DECLINE)

  score < 30: auto-approve
  score 30-70: step-up auth (3D Secure)
  score > 70: auto-decline
```

At Goldman: fail-closed (decline if fraud service unavailable). At startups: fail-open with post-hoc review. Document this as a business decision, not purely technical.

### Tricky Follow-Up Questions

**"Customer says they were charged twice. How do you investigate?"**  
Query payments by (merchant_id, amount, time_range). Check idempotency_key uniqueness. Query gateway for duplicate authorizations by external_ref. Compare ledger entries — should be exactly one DEBIT per payment_id. If duplicate found: initiate refund for duplicate, root-cause idempotency failure.

**"How do you handle partial capture?"**  
E-commerce: authorize $100, ship two items separately — capture $60 now, $40 later. Each capture is a separate ledger transaction against the same authorization. Authorization expires after 7 days (card network rule) — must capture or re-authorize.

### Technical Lead Answer Framing

> "Payment systems are a correctness problem, not a throughput problem — though you must handle both. My first principle: the ledger is append-only, double-entry, and the source of truth. I'd never update a balance column. Second: idempotency is the API contract, not an implementation detail — enforce it at the gateway with mandatory Idempotency-Key. Third: separate authorization from capture for e-commerce flows. As a lead at Goldman, I'd own the reconciliation process — that's where money silently leaks if not designed on day one."

---

## Section 11: Interview Questions & Answers

**Q1: How do you prevent double charging?**  
Three layers: (1) client sends `Idempotency-Key` header, (2) Redis cache returns cached response for duplicate key, (3) PostgreSQL UNIQUE constraint on idempotency_key rejects duplicate INSERT. Gateway also supports idempotency via its own key. All four layers together make double charge impossible.

**Q2: Explain double-entry bookkeeping in payment systems.**  
Every transaction creates equal DEBIT and CREDIT entries. Money never appears or disappears — it moves between accounts. Balance = SUM(credits) - SUM(debits). Ledger is append-only (immutable). Invariant checked on every write. Reconciliation compares our ledger against bank statements nightly.

**Q3: What happens when the payment gateway times out?**  
Never blindly retry — might double charge. Set status = PENDING_UNKNOWN. Reconciliation worker queries gateway for transaction status using our reference ID. Resolve to AUTHORIZED or FAILED based on gateway response. Alert if unresolved > 1 hour. Design gateway integration as asynchronous where possible.

**Q4: Auth vs capture — why separate?**  
Authorization holds funds on customer's card without transferring. Capture actually moves funds days later (on shipment). Allows cancellation before capture (release hold). E-commerce standard: auth at checkout, capture at fulfillment. Reduces refund volume.

**Q5: How would you scale to 100K TPS?**  
Event sourcing for ledger (append-only log, partition by account_id). CQRS: write to event log, project balances asynchronously. Shard accounts across PostgreSQL instances. Payment gateway connections pooled with async I/O. Idempotency in Redis cluster. Settlement remains batch (not real-time). At Goldman scale, custom ledger database (not off-the-shelf PostgreSQL).

---

## Section 12: Revision Notes

- **Idempotency-Key** on every write API — Redis cache + DB unique constraint
- **Double-entry ledger:** DEBIT = CREDIT per transaction; append-only; never UPDATE
- **Auth → Capture → Settle** (two-phase); refund reverses ledger entries
- **Gateway timeout → PENDING_UNKNOWN** → reconciliation worker resolves
- **Outbox pattern** for reliable Kafka events (same DB transaction)
- **PCI DSS:** tokenize cards; never store PAN; Payment Method Vault
- **10K TPS** achievable on partitioned PostgreSQL; event sourcing for 100K+
- **Active-passive** multi-region for ledger (never active-active)
- **Nightly reconciliation** with bank settlement files
- **Saga + compensation:** void on auth failure, refund on capture failure
- **Fail-closed** fraud at financial institutions; fail-open at startups

---

## Section 1: Requirements & Capacity Estimation

### Functional Requirements

### Non-Functional Requirements

| NFR | Target |
|-----|--------|
| Throughput | 1M notifications/minute peak |
| Latency (transactional) | p99 < 5 sec (OTP, payment confirmation) |

### Capacity Estimation

```
VOLUME
  1M/min = 16,667 notifications/sec peak
  80% push, 15% email, 5% SMS

PUSH (13,333/sec)
  FCM/APNs handle millions/sec — bottleneck is our service, not providers
  Each push: ~500 bytes payload

EMAIL (2,500/sec)
  SendGrid/SES: ~100/sec per account → need 25 parallel sender accounts
  Or dedicated IP pool with warmup

SMS (833/sec)
  Twilio: rate-limited per number; need number pool

STORAGE
  Notification record: ~500 bytes
  1M/min × 60 × 24 × 90 days retention = 130B records × 500B ≈ 65 TB
  Partition by created_at (monthly)
```

### High-Level Design

```
┌──────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Services    │────▶│ Notification│────▶│  Kafka Topics     │
│  (orders,    │     │ API         │     │  (by priority)    │
│   payments)  │     └─────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘
└──────────────┘                                   │
                                          ┌────────┼────────┐
                                          ▼        ▼        ▼
                                   ┌──────────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
                                   │ Push     │ │Email │ │ SMS  │
                                   │ Worker   │ │Worker│ │Worker│
                                   └────┬─────┘ └──┬───┘ └──┬───┘
                                        ▼          ▼        ▼
                                   ┌────────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
                                   │ FCM/   │ │SES/  │ │Twilio│
                                   │ APNs   │ │SendGr│ │      │
                                   └────────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘
```

### LLD — Notification Pipeline

```java
public void send(NotificationRequest req) {
    // 1. Check user preferences
    if (!preferenceService.isEnabled(req.getUserId(), req.getChannel())) return;

    // 2. Rate limit check (Redis sliding window)
    if (rateLimiter.isExceeded(req.getUserId(), req.getChannel())) {
        if (req.getPriority() != TRANSACTIONAL) return; // drop marketing
        // transactional: bypass rate limit
    }

    // 3. Render template
    String body = templateEngine.render(req.getTemplateId(), req.getVariables());

    // 4. Persist notification (PENDING)
    Notification notif = notificationRepo.save(new Notification(req, body, PENDING));

    // 5. Publish to priority-specific Kafka topic
    String topic = req.getPriority() == TRANSACTIONAL ? "notif.high" : "notif.low";
    kafkaTemplate.send(topic, req.getUserId(), notif);
}
```

**Channel workers** consume from Kafka, call external provider (FCM/SES/Twilio), update status to SENT/FAILED. Retry 3× with exponential backoff. Dead letter queue for permanent failures.

**Priority queues:** `notif.high` (transactional) consumed with more workers and lower latency SLA. `notif.low` (marketing) consumed with fewer workers; batch sends acceptable.

---

## Section 3: Scaling & Failure Handling

### Scaling

| Component | Strategy |
|-----------|----------|
| API | Stateless; horizontal auto-scale |
| Kafka | Partition by user_id; separate topics per priority |
| Push workers | 50+ instances; FCM handles fan-out |
| Email workers | Multiple sender accounts; IP warmup pool |
| SMS workers | Twilio number pool; geo-routed |
| Templates | Cache in Redis (rarely change) |
| Preferences | Redis cache per user; PostgreSQL source of truth |

### Failure Handling

| Failure | Mitigation |
|---------|------------|
| FCM/APNs down | Retry 3×; queue in Kafka (retain 7 days); alert ops |
| Email bounce | Mark email invalid; stop sending; webhook from SES |
| SMS rate limit | Rotate Twilio numbers; queue and retry |
| Template render error | Return 400 to caller; never send malformed message |
| Duplicate send | idempotency_key dedup in DB + Redis |
| Provider timeout | Status = PENDING; retry worker picks up |
| User opted out | Check preferences before send; GDPR compliance |

**Transactional vs marketing isolation:** Separate Kafka topics and worker pools. Marketing backlog never blocks OTP delivery. Circuit breaker on marketing channel if provider degraded.

---

## Section 4: Interview Questions & Answers

**Q1: How do you send 1M notifications per minute?**  
Async via Kafka. API validates + persists + publishes in < 50 ms. Workers consume and call providers in parallel. Push (FCM) handles highest volume. Email/SMS rate-limited by provider — multiple sender accounts. Priority queues ensure transactional messages not blocked.

**Q2: How do you prevent notification spam?**  
Per-user rate limit (Redis sliding window): max 10 marketing/hour, 50 push/day. User preferences (opt-out). Priority levels: transactional bypasses rate limit. Unsubscribe link in every email (CAN-SPAM/GDPR).

**Q3: How do you handle template rendering?**  
Handlebars/Mustache templates stored in PostgreSQL, cached in Redis. Variables injected at send time. Separate templates per channel (push title ≠ email body). Version templates; never modify in-use template (create new version).

**Q4: Design retry and dead letter handling.**  
Worker fails → retry 3× with backoff (1s, 5s, 30s). After 3 failures → status = FAILED, move to DLQ. DLQ dashboard for ops review. Transactional: alert on DLQ entry. Reconciliation job retries DLQ every hour.

**Q5: How do you track delivery status?**  
PUSH: FCM delivery receipt callback. EMAIL: SES webhook (delivered, bounced, opened via tracking pixel). SMS: Twilio status callback. Update notification record status. Analytics dashboard: delivery rate per channel/template.

---

## Section 5: Revision Notes

- **1M/min = 16.7K/sec** → Kafka async pipeline, not synchronous API
- **Priority queues:** transactional (high) vs marketing (low) — separate topics
- **Multi-channel:** push (FCM/APNs), email (SES), SMS (Twilio) — separate workers
- **Templates:** Handlebars with variables; cached in Redis
- **Rate limiting:** per user per channel; transactional bypasses
- **Idempotency key** prevents duplicate sends
- **User preferences** checked before every send (GDPR)
- **DLQ** for permanent failures; reconciliation job retries
- **Provider isolation:** circuit breaker per channel; marketing never blocks OTP

## Section 1: Requirements & Capacity Estimation

### Functional Requirements

### Capacity Estimation

```
QUERIES
  100K QPS peak
  Avg query: 3 words × 5 bytes = 15 bytes in; response ~5 KB out
  Bandwidth: 100K × 5 KB = 500 MB/sec

INDEX SIZE
  10B documents × avg 10 KB indexed text = 100 TB raw
  Inverted index overhead (~30%): ~130 TB
  Sharded across 500 Elasticsearch nodes → 260 GB/node

WRITES (indexing)
  10K new documents/sec (bulk updates)
  Each doc: tokenize → stem → add to inverted index

AUTOCOMPLETE
  50K QPS (5× search QPS)
  Served from trie cache in Redis — sub-ms latency
```

## Section 2: Design (APIs, Database, HLD, LLD)

### APIs

```http
GET  /api/v1/search?q={query}&page=1&size=20&filters=category:books,price:10-50

GET  /api/v1/search/{docId}              # document detail

```

### Search Response

```json
{
  "query": "spring boot microservices",
  "totalHits": 45230,
  "took_ms": 45,

    {
```

### Index Structure — Inverted Index

```
Term          → Postings List (doc_id, term_frequency, positions)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
"spring"      → [(doc_1, 5, [0,12,45]), (doc_7, 2, [3,88]), (doc_23, 8, [1,5,9,...])]
"boot"        → [(doc_1, 3, [1,13]), (doc_7, 1, [4]), ...]
"microservice"→ [(doc_1, 12, [2,15,20,...]), (doc_15, 4, [0,30]), ...]
```

Each postings list sorted by doc_id. At query time: intersect postings lists for AND queries; union for OR queries.

### Database / Storage Design

| Component | Technology | Purpose |
|-----------|-----------|---------|
| Inverted index | Elasticsearch (Lucene) | Full-text search + ranking |
| Document store | PostgreSQL / MongoDB | Source of truth for documents |
| Autocomplete trie | Redis | Prefix → top suggestions |
| Spell check dictionary | Redis / Bloom filter | "Did you mean" corrections |
| Analytics | Kafka → ClickHouse | Query logs for ranking tuning |

```json
// Elasticsearch document mapping
{
  "doc_id": "doc_123",
  "title": "Spring Boot Microservices Guide",
  "body": "Full text content...",
  "category": "books",
  "price": 29.99,
  "created_at": "2026-01-15",
  "popularity_score": 0.85
}
```

### High-Level Design

```
┌──────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│  Client  │────▶│ Search API  │────▶│ Query Processor  │
└──────────┘     └─────────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘
                                              │
                    ┌─────────────────────────┼──────────────┐
                    ▼                         ▼              ▼
            ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────┐
            │ Elasticsearch│         │ Redis Trie   │  │ Spell    │
            │ Cluster      │         │ (autocomplete)│  │ Checker  │
            │ (inverted    │         └──────────────┘  └──────────┘
            │  index)      │
            └──────────────┘
                    ▲
                    │ index updates
            ┌───────┴──────┐
            │ Indexer Svc  │◀── Kafka (doc.created, doc.updated)
            └──────────────┘
```

### LLD — Query Processing Pipeline

```java
public SearchResponse search(String query, Filters filters, int page, int size) {
    // 1. Tokenize and normalize query
    List<String> terms = tokenizer.tokenize(query);  // lowercase, remove stop words
    terms = terms.stream().map(stemmer::stem).collect(toList());

    // 2. Spell check (if low results expected)
    String corrected = spellChecker.correct(query);

    // 3. Build Elasticsearch query
    BoolQueryBuilder esQuery = QueryBuilders.boolQuery()
        .should(QueryBuilders.matchQuery("title", query).boost(3.0f))
        .should(QueryBuilders.matchQuery("body", query).boost(1.0f))
        .filter(buildFilters(filters));

    // 4. Execute with pagination
    SearchHits hits = esClient.search(esQuery, page, size);

    // 5. Post-process: highlight snippets, compute facets
    return buildResponse(hits, corrected);
}
```

### Ranking (BM25 + Signals)

```
score(doc, query) = BM25(doc, query) × popularity_boost × freshness_boost

BM25(doc, query) = Σ IDF(term) × (TF × (k1+1)) / (TF + k1 × (1 - b + b × |doc|/avgdl))

popularity_boost = log(1 + click_count)
freshness_boost = 1 / (1 + days_since_created × 0.01)
```

Elasticsearch uses BM25 by default. Custom boosts for title match (3×), exact phrase match (5×), popularity signal.

### Indexing Pipeline

```
Document created/updated in source DB
  → CDC (Debezium) or application event → Kafka
  → Indexer Service consumes:
      tokenize → stem → remove stop words → compute term frequencies
      → bulk index to Elasticsearch (batch 1000 docs/request)
  → Near-real-time: ES refresh interval 1 sec
```

---

## Section 3: Scaling & Failure Handling

### Scaling

| Component | Strategy |
|-----------|----------|
| Elasticsearch | 500 shards; 3 replicas; shard by doc_id hash |
| Query service | Stateless; 100+ instances behind load balancer |
| Autocomplete | Redis trie; replicated; 50K QPS sub-ms |
| Indexing | Kafka partitioned by doc_id; 50 indexer workers |
| Caching | Redis cache for top 1000 popular queries (5 min TTL) |

### Failure Handling

| Failure | Mitigation |
|---------|------------|
| ES node down | Replica serves queries; auto-rebalance shards |
| Stale index | Acceptable up to 1 min; indexer catches up from Kafka |
| Slow query (> 500 ms) | Timeout; return partial results; log for optimization |
| Index corruption | Rebuild from source DB + Kafka replay |
| Autocomplete miss | Fall back to prefix search on ES (slower but functional) |
| Zero results | Spell correction suggestion; relaxed query (OR instead of AND) |

---

## Section 4: Interview Questions & Answers

**Q1: How does an inverted index work?**  
Each term maps to a postings list of (doc_id, term_frequency, positions). Query "spring boot": intersect postings lists for "spring" AND "boot". Return doc_ids ranked by TF-IDF/BM25 score. Enables O(postings) lookup instead of scanning all documents.

**Q2: How do you rank search results?**  
BM25 (probabilistic TF-IDF) as base score. Boost title matches 3×, exact phrases 5×. Multiply by popularity (click-through rate) and freshness decay. ML re-ranking layer (LambdaMART) for top 100 candidates at Google/Amazon scale. Start with BM25 for interviews.

**Q3: Design autocomplete/typeahead.**  
Trie (prefix tree) in Redis. Each node stores top 10 suggestions by popularity. On keystroke, traverse trie → return suggestions in < 1 ms. Updated nightly from search logs. Separate from full search to avoid ES load on every keystroke.

**Q4: How do you handle 10B documents?**  
Elasticsearch with 500 shards (~20M docs/shard). Shard by hash(doc_id). 3 replicas for read scaling and fault tolerance. Index only searchable fields (not full document). Source of truth in PostgreSQL; ES is derived view.

**Q5: Near-real-time indexing at 10K docs/sec?**  
Kafka buffers document changes. Indexer workers batch 1000 docs per bulk ES request. ES refresh interval = 1 sec (near-real-time). CDC from source DB ensures no missed updates. Reindex job for full rebuild if corruption.

---

## Section 5: Revision Notes

- **Inverted index:** term → postings list (doc_id, TF, positions)
- **BM25 ranking** with title boost (3×), popularity, freshness
- **100K QPS** → ES cluster (500 shards, 3 replicas) + query cache
- **Autocomplete:** Redis trie, separate from full search
- **Indexing:** Kafka → indexer → ES bulk API; 1 sec refresh
- **10B docs ≈ 130 TB** index; shard by hash(doc_id)
- **Spell correction** on zero/low results
- **Faceted search** via ES aggregations
- **Source of truth** in PostgreSQL; ES is derived/rebuildable

> **Reading Time:** ~15 minutes | **Page Equivalent:** ~6 pages

## Section 1: Requirements & Capacity Estimation

### Functional Requirements

| # | Requirement |
|---|-------------|
| F1 | Track inventory quantity per SKU per warehouse |
| F2 | Reserve inventory on order placement |
| F3 | Confirm reservation on payment success |
| F4 | Release reservation on payment failure / cancellation |
| F5 | Deduct inventory on shipment |
| F6 | Restock (warehouse receiving) |
| F7 | Low-stock alerts and reorder triggers |
| F8 | Inventory inquiry across warehouses (ATP — Available to Promise) |

### Non-Functional Requirements

| NFR | Target |
|-----|--------|
| Consistency | Never oversell (available ≥ 0 at all times) |
| Latency | p99 < 100 ms for reserve operation |
| Availability | 99.99% |
| Throughput | 50K reservations/sec peak (Prime Day) |
| Accuracy | Inventory count accurate to ±0 (not approximate) |

### Capacity Estimation

```
RESERVATIONS
  50K/sec peak (Amazon Prime Day)
  Each reservation: ~200 bytes (sku, warehouse, qty, order_id, ttl)
  Bandwidth: 50K × 200B = 10 MB/sec

STORAGE
  10M SKUs × 500 warehouses = 5B inventory records
  Per record: ~100 bytes (sku, warehouse, on_hand, reserved, available)
  Total: 5B × 100B = 500 GB (fits in Redis cluster with PostgreSQL backing)

WRITES
  Reserve: 50K/sec → must be atomic per SKU-warehouse
  Confirm/release: ~50K/sec (matching order flow)
  Restock: 1K/sec (batch, less frequent)
```
